utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this Monday, 24 September, we are starting again our hearings this week. I greet Mr. Scott and the counsel and the accused and all people in this room, this courtroom. As we know, we have this week a witness who is coming to bear testimony for three days. I will be obliged to leave around noon if the examination does not end because there is a Plenary of the Judges for the mission of the president of the Tribunal, so it would be Judge Prandler who will preside over this Chamber in the afternoon Wednesday day, next Wednesday. That is what I wanted to tell you. I understand that Mr. Karnavas wishes to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. Good afternoon Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon everyone. My remarks concern the upcoming witness, Mr. Miller, or Professor Miller. I am somewhat concerned, and I want to bring something to the Court's attention at this point in time. My remarks will primarily deal with the second part of his -- the second so-called report that he prepared dealing with post -- you know, the persistence of Herceg-Bosna after Washington Agreement and Dayton. Now, I look at the decision that was rendered by the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber indicated that it would hear the witness's testimony and then determine the relevance and probative value. That's the very last part. Now, we've been at trial for 17 months. The indictment is rather comprehensive. We know that it ends sometime in 1994. Now the gentleman is going to be talking about events that occurred in 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, all the way to the present time, I presume, and it would seem to me that in the past when an accused such as -- or a counsel for an accused has stood up to go into areas which were outside the scope of the indictment, the Trial Chamber rightfully pointed out that one need not go into those areas because they were not relevant. They were outside the indictment. Now, we filed a joint response on July 3rd. Preceding that, the Stojic Defence on the 20th of June had non-opposed but then later on 3 July they joined with the joint opposition to this particular report and to the relevancy of this matter. Here's my concern, Mr. President and Your Honours, that by going into this area, and I am perfectly happy to go into it if we have several weeks. We're going to be turning this trial into some kind of a symposium on post conflict reconstruction in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Anyone who has worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina since Dayton knows that you have countless NGOs. You have the office of the High Representative, you have the UN, the OSCE, you have all these folks that are -- they are trying to make sense of that country. You have laws being passed in every canton to every -- to the entities, you have impositions of laws, and so on and so forth. And it seems to me that you cannot judge this era and say that the Croats are doing this or that without looking at everyone, and I'm talking everyone, starting with the UN, starting with the office of the High Representative, starting with what the Republika Srpska is doing, what Bosniaks are doing, as well as the Croats. And so while it might be a fascinating seminar since 2005 after 10 years of Dayton there have been attempts to modify the constitution of BiH because they have concluded that Dayton was good to stop the war but was terrible for the peace in the sense of getting this country going. This is an ongoing process, and I fear that if we hear this sort of evidence, you will in essence be opening up a Pandora's box. Now, I don't -- I don't mind spending a few days with this particular historian here, but I need to know concretely at what point in time will the Trial Chamber make its determination as to whether this evidence, whatever it might be, is relevant to the case and whether it has any probative value, but relevance in particular is what concerns me, because if you are going to wait until the conclusion of the trial, you are forcing the Defence to in essence mount a defence on post-Dayton reconstruction in BiH. And it's not enough to say don't, Well don't worry, we're professional Judges. We know what to do. That is not an answer, because we are entitled to know what it is that we are defending against. Are we defending against the indictment, or are we defending against everything and anything no matter what the time or place, and that's why I need some guidance. Will we know at the end of the testimony whether the Trial Chamber will find it relevant because then we will need to re-evaluate how we're going to proceed at some point. But I dare say it is a gross error for this Trial Chamber to be going into a time period into matters that are outside the scope of the indictment. It is unfair to the Defence. It might be interesting, but it's terribly unfair to the Defence and it's not what I consider a proper usage of time. If the Trial Chamber, as it has indicated, is concerned for the well-being of the accused, especially as far as the time it takes to try this case, and it has noted on several occasions that we need to have expedited and efficient usage of time in court which is why sometimes the cross-examination time is curtailed. If that is the case, then I think that this is one instance when the Trial Chamber should refrain from wasting a whole weeks of time hearing testimony that is not relevant because you can just see from the dates, you know. And getting back to one other point which is connected to this, we have still to hear from the Prosecution there are answer as to whether we need to defend against Ahmici. Mr. Scott stood up at one point and said he needed to consult with Mr. Stringer, and I want to bring to the Court's attention that at the time that this case was started or at the time that the indictment was drafted, during the pre-trial phase, during the beginning of the trial, Mr. Stringer was not there. He had nothing to do with the indictment. So why all of a sudden we need to get Mr. Stringer's advice as to whether something that's in the document or maybe not in the document is something that the Defence has to defend against. Maybe Mr. Mundis can help Mr. Scott. I don't care, but I think this goes -- this ties in with what I'm saying today. We need clear guidance. What is it are we defending against? Is it against the entire post Dayton events in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Because there are a thousand different opinions. It depends on where you are and who you talk to. And you're opening up a Pandora's box. So I would like some guidance. I think the Trial Chamber can provide some guidance especially before we hear the direct examination, but I certainly think it would be terribly unfair to say let's wait until the end of the trial to decide as we did with Donia when 5th century history is relevant because then you force us to call witnesses and to mount a defence against 5th and 10th century history that has nothing to do with the events from 1991 and 1994. So these are my remarks, Mr. President. I trust that and I would hope that you would consult with your colleagues and perhaps give us some guidance. I understand the decision, but I think it's one thing to say I'm going to hear the evidence and then determine what weight, if any, to give to it. But when it comes to relevance that's something that we need to know right up front. I don't think we need to hear the entire testimony to determine whether events 1997 or 1998 or events concerning Mr. Jelavic, who is not even over here, have something to do with this particular case. I don't think we need to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On which you've just mentioned, the Chamber has discussed the matter starting with the report of the 9 pages report, and 28 footnotes in particular, the persistence of the Herceg-Bosna and -- after the accords of Dayton and Washington he drafted 9 pages which are directly linked to paragraph 26 of the Prosecution's briefs in July 2007 in which the Prosecutor wrote this which I'm going to read slowly: "The second report of Mr. Miller concerns also directly the thesis of the Prosecution according to which Herceg-Bosna was not an association or a group of citizens which was of provisional character but which had been established either in order to have a permanent state opposed to the government of Sarajevo or as a victor of a great Croatia, federated to the Republic of Croatia, or being part of it. The admissibility of this evidence doesn't depend on what the Prosecution thinks. The non-dissolution of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna long times after Washington and Bosna Accords destroys all argument according to which it was -- it would have been a temporary association having no sinister intention against the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Other evidence such as confidential minutes confirm that republic of Bosna-Herceg was still part of the same plan and posed problems, permanent problems, for the international community and had as a consequence a climate of violence in the region." So this is the approach of the Prosecution on this matter which was detailed at paragraph 26 of its motion of July 27 -- 2007. This is directly connected with the second part of Mr. Miller's report which takes up nine pages. So the Chamber which has understood all these problems and your opposition has made a decision, and indicated in this decision that because of this testimony of the witness the Chamber will appraise the probative value and the relevance and will decide on the question to know whether these reports can be admitted. Maybe what is said by the Prosecution in paragraph 26 is completely false or wrong but we will only know that after having heard Mr. Miller and after having heard the cross-examination. This is all we can say now. So, Mr. Karnavas, this question has been studied and debated by the members of the Chamber at length, because we were expecting the Defence to contest this, take issue on this. So we are now going to have the witness. Please, usher, will you introduce Mr. Miller.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, first of all good afternoon to everyone and to the Trial Chamber. While -- or, rather, before the witness is brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the English? Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom, especially to the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, while we're having the witness shown in may I just table a request for prolonging the deadline to a response to the Prosecution submission of the 20th of September, because they requested the introduction of a documentary, a set of documents, 539 documents in all linked to Herceg-Bosna, and the topic is the HVO as the political military and administrative structure, and I'd like to tell the Trial Chamber that that means more than 4.000 documents which means a lot of hard work for the Defence teams, and according to the deadlines from the rules of evidence we are supposed to reply by the 4th of October. But Your Honours, may we be given a 10 to 15 days' grace period for us to be able to review that? So could you extend the deadline? You know that we are inundated with many documents and this would be an additional burden and at the 65 ter Conference let me just remind you the Prosecution was very fair in informing us about the plans, its plans, and this helped us in our own planning, but this particular submission was not planned, at least not in that volume. It's a very serious submission. We have reviewed it preliminarily and within reason we would need another fortnight to look through the documents and then respond. So please could you extend that deadline, and we shall be responding all together, all the Defence teams together, and of course this is a question that we have is to consult our clients with because some decisions just can't be made without our clients. Through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might -- if I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you if I might respond ever so briefly. Your Honour, first of all Your Honour to jump to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, technical point. On line 24 of page 7, Mr. Kovacic is having spoken of more than 4.000 documents, should it rather not be more than 4.000 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, pages. That's right, Your Honour. The -- I quoted name of the document 539 documents and these were pages, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just very briefly just to jump to the bottom line the Prosecution does not object to the request of additional time, number one. I just do want the record to be clear, however, I'm not attributing anything -- any ill will other than perhaps faulty memory which I'm increasingly prone to my self, this was the plan filing as the transcript excerpt that we provided to the Chamber some days ago. We had indicated in July the filings that we would make between that time and the end of September, and this filing was one of the specific filings discussed. The only thing that's different about it is we substantially reduced the number of total documents that we expected to tender. But the transcript is quite clear. The Court may remember that at one point the Prosecution thought that we could make such a filing immediately following the recess on approximately the 16th of August if we were granted relief from one of the guideline requirements. The Chamber did not grant us that relief, and we did the additional work and we said at the time in July that if the -- that relief weren't granted that filing would be made approximately the end of September or early October, and we indeed filed it on the 20th of September. So just so the record is clear, it was planned -- it was specifically anticipated and planned, and we did better than expected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. A small request. Today is the deadline for responding to the Prosecution's request to introduce certain documentary evidence from the Vares municipality area. All six Defence teams are preparing a joint respond but that response is composed in 3.709 words. So with your permission we would like to be allowed to respond with more words. The number is -- let me it right in the transcript. The total number of words is 3.709. 3.709. Yes that's correct thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are two requests for the number of words. The Chamber will allow Ms. Alaburic's request for the number of words edited for the directive. Secondly, as for the time to answer the 539 documents, the Chamber is minded to give 15 supplementary days. We are now going to have the witness in the courtroom. I will give the floor to the registrar who will give us certain number of -- who will give us certain numbers for the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, several of the parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness C. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 666, the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 667, the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 668, and the list submitted by 5D shall be given the Exhibit number IC 669.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] Thank you. If you hear what I in English please say you understand what I have you've said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give your name, first name, and birth date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Nick Miller I was born on 6 October 1963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a professor of history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Boise State University in Idaho in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in court on the facts which happened in ex-Yugoslavia or is it the very first time you come to bear witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my first time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the text of the solemn declaration aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You can take a seat. So, sir, a few explanations about this hearing, which not surprise you since you are an historian and American citizen. Common law procedure is known to you. You will first of all have to answer to the questions of the Prosecution, Mr. Scott, which you probably have already met during the weekend, and Mr. Scott will ask questions from you on the two reports which you have drafted for the Chamber. At the end of this examination chief -- in chief for about three hours, the counsel of Defence which are on your left-hand side, there are many of them but each of them represents one of the accused, possibly also the accused themselves may also ask questions for you -- from you during your cross-examination, what we call the cross-examination. The four Judges of the Bench which you can see, I know that in your country it's rather exceptional to hear a Judge asking questions in criminal proceedings, but here our Rules of Procedure enable us to do so. We may also ask questions from you in order to understand better or enlighten some of your answers. As a rule we prefer to wait for the end of the examination of both parties or cross-examination, but since we have the documents here in order to save time we follow up and we then can avoid to have to do -- search documents in future. If at any time you don't feel well or you wish to have a break don't hesitate to tell us. And since you will answer in English to questions asked by Mr. Scott or by the Defence teams in English, please pause between the end of the question and the beginning of your answer so that the interpreters may have the time to translate into French and B/C/S for the accused what you will have answered. If at any time you wish to ask a question from the members of the Chamber don't hesitate. We can also countenance them and answer. Broadly this is how this hearing will go on, which is supposed to go on for three days. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and once again, good afternoon to all the Judges and to all those in and about the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also good afternoon, Mr. Miller.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of the day I may refer to you as Dr. Miller. I know I just said Mr. You'll forgive me if I'm not completely consistent on that point, but we will cover here just momentarily a bit of your educational and professional background for purposes of your testimony here today and in the next few days. In that regard, is it correct that you received a master's degree in history from Indiana University in 1987?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a doctorate or Ph.D. from the same university in 1991, also in history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you have been employed teaching history at the Boise State University since 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I understand and congratulate you that since the 1st of August this year you are the Chair of the history department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us within the field of history what are your particular areas of work or expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. I was trained at Indiana in the history of the Balkans, broadly. But in graduate school we're compelled to focus ever more on smaller and smaller pieces of the puzzle. So at this point on I teach courses on the Balkans on former Yugoslavia on nationalism in Europe. My research focus has been on Croatian and Serbian history. Over the past 20 years I've have travelled throughout the country, where it's the parts of the former country, but my expertise is generally Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct Dr. Miller that you have taught a number of courses on -- as you just indicated eastern Europe, history of Yugoslavia, European nationalism, history of the Balkans and such courses as those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Those courses are part of my primary teaching focus. I teach them regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in addition is it correct that you have written and published extensively on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes that, true too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one thing that I noticed in your CV, and I'm certainly not going through all the details, but I believe everyone in the courtroom would have seen it previously as part of the filings that were made. You indicated that in 1988, 1989, you were involved with something called the International Exchange Board Research Fellowship to Yugoslavia. Can you tell us briefly what that involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. IREX or the international exchanges and research board is an organisation that once funded doctoral and post-doctoral research to eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. And so in 1988 and 1989 I went to former Yugoslavia to work on my dissertation and spent six months in Zagreb, five or six months in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, we're going to move fairly quickly, hopefully. And without further introduction I would like to turn to the two reports that you have prepared in connection with this case, and I assume you probably have those in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm showing you first of all -- if the binder -- if the exhibits could be provided to the witness it might as well be now I suppose. I am afraid that there are three binders and bundle altogether, although some of the documents -- a number of the documents we won't in fact be focusing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My thanks to the usher for the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, just to start, and I see you have one there and it may be easier for you to use the loose one, if I can say that, rather than what's in the binder for these particular purposes. But your report that is titled "The Characteristics and Patterns of the Balkan Conflict as Widely Known and Reported by the Latter Part of 1992," that has been given the Exhibit number P 10239, and you have that report in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you then prepared a second report which is titled: "The Persistence of Herceg-Bosna after the Washington Agreement and Dayton"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that has been marked as Exhibit P 10240. And do you also have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, these reports I think that were finalised and dated on the 7th of June, 2007. Can I just ask you, do you continue to stand behind the content and observations of those reports today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that if I took you in considerably more detail through both reports, more than I actually intend to in court, that the content of those two reports would be your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can start with the report which is Exhibit P 10239, "The Characteristics and Patterns of the Balkan Conflict." What I'd like to do, Dr. Miller, is ask you just at various places throughout your report if you can just clarify or perhaps amplify a few things. My first question to you is: If you look at the first page of your report, not the cover, not the title page, but the actual first page of actual text. Let me see if by way of introduction I can state the questions that were essentially posed to you. Is it correct that the first question that you were asked to research or look into, if you will, was to inquire whether any particular characteristics or patterns or might be called features of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia in connection with the dissolution of that country - which you made reference to a couple of moments ago - whether there were such observable characteristics, practices or features? Is that one of the questions that you were asked to look at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first basic question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the second and related question, were you asked to research to what extent those characteristics, practices or features to the extent that you concluded that there were, were reported in the local, regional, national and international media and other -- by other means would have become known to the general public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That was the second aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you then to look if you would -- you give us a summary in your report on the first page and just by way of further introduction, if I can ask you to look at what you list as A, B, and C, and could I just ask you to read your -- the three basic conclusions that you've listed as A, B, and C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. Conclusion A is that the civilian toll of acts of persecution attacks and forcible population transfers was in fact widely known in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992. B, the second conclusion, the attempt to subjugate populations and take territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to slow down a little bit for the interpreters and the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The attempt to subjugate populations or take territory was substantially likely to result in violence against civilians, including killings, widespread destruction, forced expulsions, and other criminal acts. And C, that such acts were already manifested during the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina by and beyond the latter part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And now the -- immediately following that you indicate that a particular focus then was "the depth and breadth of public knowledge both in the former Yugoslavia and more generally of the characteristics and practices." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you say about what you mean when you say "a particular focus was on the depth and breadth of public knowledge"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was trying to examine how much an average person would know about what was happening in the wars in Croatia and early on in Bosnia. By depth and breadth I meant by how widely knowledge would have spread but also -- well, how in-depth that knowledge would be. So in other words did people just have a superficial knowledge of what was going on or in some cases did they have a more profound understanding. So I was examining those two aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now continuing to the bottom of the first page, you continue to make reference to "Political developments after the death of Tito in 1980 made ethnic differentiation and conflict the norm." I would like you to explain, please, something about the political developments that you referred to there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when Tito died in 1980 he left behind a country without -- he had not established a leadership transition so there was nobody in place to, I suppose you could say, guide the country in the way he might have hoped it would be, so there was a vacuum, a leadership vacuum. The economy of Yugoslavia was also getting worse. I guess it was in a shambles already but the standard of living was declining and the politicians who were left to try to solve these problems, it couldn't. And so by the mid-1980s at the earliest we see the emergence of political leaders or potential political leaders who, unable to deal with what I would call real problems, turn to their populations and attempt to mobilise them on a more visceral level and the -- as a result politics in the late 1980s became quite nationalistic, ethnic, if you will. So I guess my general point is that when Tito died having left nothing behind to sort of follow his path, politicians turned to their own ethnic groups for power instead of -- instead of maintaining politics on an all-Yugoslav level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on with similar questions on the top of page 2, and I believe that you're referring to someone else's work, but nonetheless the phrase is used, "The reduction of political discourse to ethnicity." Can you tell us your understanding of what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. What is meant by that is that -- let's see. I'll put this in my own words. If -- if there was a problem in Yugoslavia that had a solution, let's say that the economy was failing and there was some kind of economic approach that could be taken, by the end of the 1980s that economic approach would not be taken and instead politicians would blame their own people's or region's economic failures or economic inadequacies is on something ethnic. So we find for instance in the economic sphere by that time that the Croats would blame the Serbs for exploiting the Croatian tourist economy, the Serbs had blamed the Croats for exploiting Serbia's raw materials production. Sorry. And so by reduction of -- of political discourse to ethnicity, I mean that ethnicity became the single key as most Yugoslav politicians understood it. They would reduce everything to that instead of examining -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. You said that upon Tito's death, since he had not foreseen transition, the political parties turned to ethnic questions. But another aspect comes to mind, and I have not heard it much discussed during these almost two years of trial. When Tito died, what of the Yugoslav Communist Party? Did that party -- was it not supposed to ensure the transition without having to resort to ethnic issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would have been, I think, the chosen response. What I meant by Tito not arranging a succession was that -- well, he was quite jealous of his own power. There probably was one chosen successor, a gentleman named Edvard Kardelj, but he died the year before Tito died, and so you know when Tito did die, he left behind a situation that frankly a lot of dictators left behind which is that there was nobody to take his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me Your Honour I notice some vocal reaction in the courtroom that I think is entirely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's okay. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Doctor, but it's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that someone had been designated as a possible successor for President Tito and unfortunately died before Tito, and the Presiding Judge already raised the issue of the Communist Party. My question is well, what did the constitution foresee? Did it not foresee any legal mechanisms to deal with the death of President Tito.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. This is all tied up in one question and I'm sorry I didn't finish my answer. What was established before Tito died was a collective Presidency and collective party leadership that would rotate between republics and provinces. So one of them was on a two year rotation one on a three year rotation, I can't recall which one was which. But the idea then was that the party, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, would provide for a succession on a rotating basis. The problem was that there is a lack of a sort executive power or direction in that type of situation, and so the economy and the political system were basically treading water for five or six, seven years until -- until local politicians decided to exert themselves. And this is where we see Slobodan Milosevic, for instance, after 1988 sort taking the bull by the horns so to speak in Serbian politics to -- but that period after Tito died was one of aimlessness, and I think it's thanks to the solution that was imposed, the collective solution, rotating solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on to the following paragraph, the first paragraph beginning on page 2. Again I'm going to ask you just about a number of terms and phrases that are used. You used the term "particularist nationalisms." Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, "particularist nationalisms" are juxtaposed with the Yugoslav idea in actual quote, and so particular nationalisms would be nationalisms that emphasize the local nations in questions. So a particularist nationalism would be Croat or Serbian or Slovene or others juxtaposed with the Yugoslav idea which is a notion that is supra-national, I suppose, that argues that all of the peoples of Yugoslavia or most of them are actually members of a larger more general nation. The Yugoslav idea was never deeply rooted in Yugoslavia itself. But once Tito died the emphasis on that more particular nationalisms become more and more acute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to the bottom of that same page you -- you also make the statement then that in the case of the wars of Yugoslav succession, though, civilians became a particular focus of the attention of warring parties. Could you tell us again more about that and let me just say that it might be suggested that your report is largely saying perhaps not a lot more than that there wars are bad, bad things happen in war, and civilians often get unfortunately have bad things happen to them in war. Is that basically the nature of your paper, or is your paper different and further than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would argue -- I would agree that civilians tend to always be victims in a war, especially 19th and 20th century wars. But in this case -- in this case the purpose of all of the various wars of all the wars in Yugoslavia are to separate people on a national or ethnic basis and when that is one of the goals of the actual warfare, civilians are no longer just occasional or accidental victims. They actually become part of the solution -- I'm sorry I'll try to remember to slow down. As such, in the wars in Yugoslavia, moving civilians around either by killing them or perhaps just forcing them out of the regions in which they live was an actual goal. It wasn't incidental.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also toward the end of that -- excuse me. Maybe no. Let me just -- excuse me. I lost my place. I'm jumping to page 4. I think that's why I lost my place because I was jumping quite a bit over to page 4. And toward the bottom of that page you talk about extremist paramilitaries on both sides. The bottom of the page. Extremist militaries on both sides had already begun to move aside the peacemakers, and I was wondering if you could tell the Judges what you observed in preparing your report, if anything, about the phenomenon by which the more extreme elements tended to displace or -- or move out the more moderate elements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that basically that more extreme elements are able to -- to win out in situations like this because they're willing to use more extreme measures. In the particular case of Yugoslavia, populations had been prepared since 1988, 1989, perhaps earlier to believe the more extreme explanation to any given set of events in which -- I mean so -- so you know, psychologically I think the population was in a position where it would believe the worst, which is -- which plays into the hands of extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Going on to page 5 about the first paragraph beginning on page 5. In that sentence you say ethnicity was the fuel of conflict in the former Yugoslavia and territorial and conquest and cleansing was the goal. And I'd like to divide that in two parts. Perhaps you've touched on this already, but when you say "Ethnicity was the fuel of conflict," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again I just -- I mean that politicians who were governing in the given republics in Yugoslavia, some to a greater extent than others, had grown used to using their ethnic groups to further their political interests. Yugoslavs had grown to thinking in purely local ethnic terms. And the goals of the warring sides even of the warring sides that we don't think of as particularly extremists were ethnic. So Slovenia was trying to establish a Slovenian state that was essentially pure, the Serbs and the Croats were doing the same. So ethnicity, ethnic distrust, or even hatred is the fuel in that sense. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the second part you actually just touched on. I thought you had actually moved on to the -- that territorial conquest and cleansing was the goal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all right, I guess I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you anything more to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think I did, I think I did answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look at Exhibit in the -- one of the bundles there, Exhibit P 10271. And it may be -- I'm guessing it's in your -- it's going to be in the third bundles, the third binder of the ones you have, the smaller of the three binders. Might be able to -- if I can assist people in the courtroom, the first two large binders are primarily, if not all together I believe, presidential transcripts which are -- most of which are not going to be used, and the one or two that will be used will be toward the end of the examination. So it may assist if people don't have to worry about moving these two large binders around for the time being. Were you able to find Exhibit P 10271?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could just look at that and actually it's a compilation -- well, it's a combination of two separate articles. They could have just as easily I suppose have been two exhibits, but they were put together as one. Are these the type of open source or media material that you researched and looked at in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I took what I thought was a very straightforward approach which was to look at the most prominent journals in Croatia and Serbia at the time. This is from Danas which was considered a reliable source for news in Croatia and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the second article is from what publication? In the same bundle. They're both from Danas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're both from Danas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry I was looking ahead. My apology. Would you tell me when you looked at that sort of material, and you footnoted those particular articles in your first report, I mean, what did you see in those reports that caused them -- you to think that these were illustrative or gave substance to some of the points that you were seeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, in both cases they are dealing with incidents in Borovo Selo or in Eastern Slavonia in general, and they are both just relatively straightforward recountings of what happened at the time. You could find actually much more blood-curdling accounts of these events but these are not that. These are rather modest and since they both -- since they were published in Danas, and I just took them to be rather basic examples of what the average Croat might know about at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These articles were published when? Can you assist the Chamber in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that these articles were published at what might be considered in the overall Balkan conflict quite early in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite early the conflict arguably began before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I asked you this, perhaps you've answered this but let me just be clear. I take it from you what you said previously that these didn't stand out as being particularly unique, but did you find those to be essentially representative of the type of media accounts that you saw in the literature during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were representative of -- of -- yes, they were. There were more - as I said - there were there were more elaborate descriptions of what happened. I would call these fairly -- fairly down-to-earth descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to page 7 of your report. On the top of that page when you get it -- by this part in the report you're beginning to on some extent focus on different types of conduct or behaviour or phenomenon if you will. At the top of page 7 you say "The barbarous treatment of captives was another common theme of the press coverage of the Croatian war." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that regard can I ask you to look at if you can find Exhibit P 10272. Which is titled -- it's actually referenced in footnote 13 of your report entitled "The Army is Washing its Hands." Can you tell us briefly what that is an account of if you will or report about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This particular account comes from Vreme which was I guess to put it generally a Serbian counterpart to Danas in that neither of those two magazines were in the hands of a political party. They both were sort of generally accepted as providing a -- a relatively balanced view. In this case the author is describing the actions of a couple of paramilitary organisations based in Belgrade which were rather busy in Eastern Slavonia again -- I don't know how to put it, doing horrifying things to civilians. The fact that this is Serbian groups being described by the Serbian press to my mind makes it at least on the surface a -- a believable account. There was plenty in the press attributing the most horrifying acts to other ethnic groups, but this is a Serbian case describing Serbian actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this was an article written in March 1992 but in fact about an event that apparently occurred in October 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For purposes of staying on this same topic of captives or persons who have been detained or detentions, I'd like to jump to page 15 of your report please and we'll come back. By the time you've reached page 15 of your report, at the top of that page you say: "Whereas nearly all of the behaviour reported by Mazowiecki and his informants replicated behaviour from the Croatian war during 1991, two aspects of the Bosnian situation differed. First, the widespread existence of detention camps," and then there's a parenthetical, "and second the use of rape as a systematic tool of warfare by all sides." Now I'm not focusing on the second part by now, but in connection to the widespread use of detention camps, I wonder if you can tell the Judges whether based on again the open-source literature at the time it was reported that there were camps at this time not only operated by the JNA or the Serbs but camps or detention operations or facilities being operated by all three of the principal ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that these two articles one from Danas, another from Vreme, both note publicly that there were Serbian camps being operated as well as Croatian camps on the territory of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you refer to -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I'm not sure if any of these are Muslim camps, but nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now when you referred -- I'm sorry. You referred just now to the articles -- you're referring to those that we can find in your text on page 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. The article from Danas is called "Teror pasa I cuvara" and the article from Vreme, "To Each his own Camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at Exhibit P 10276?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that the article called in English "To Each his own Camp"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll give everyone in the courtroom a chance to find that. In the first full paragraph of text under the headings and the bold print, in the middle of that paragraph it says "The International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC, whose representatives have visited over 4300 prisoners of all sides in the conflict since the organisation resumed its activities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, certainly know about the camps; although, 'The ICRC has not been permitted to visit many detention centres scattered all over the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.'" And then down in the next paragraph about five lines down you'll see the language it says, "Proves that camps exist only all sides." And as part of your research would you be able to say that that is consistent with what the various reports that there were camps being operated on all sides as far as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By August of 1992? By the time of this writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In you report going on to the next page of the article, at least in the English translation, there are references to camps and prisons being in Mostar, Ljubuski, Livno, and Capljina. Did you come to understand some of the camps that were being operated in 1992 were being operated by Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I would assume that those camps that were on territory controlled by the HVO were controlled by Croats, and I think that's the understanding that we see in the article and in other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to the second article that you also mention which is Exhibit P 10277.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that an article that appeared in the San Francisco Chronicle on the 15th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Titled "Serbs Also are Victims in Bosnian War/Croats Holding Children, Women in Detention Camps."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just briefly looking down at that can you make reference to the camps that were being discussed primarily in this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camps described in this article again are Ljubuski, looks like Capljina. In other words, on territory of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I said I skipped quite a bit ahead. Let me go back to page 7 of your report, please. In the second paragraph on that page I'm turning now we've touched a bit on detentions and camps, and I'm touching a bit now on question of refugees. And in the second paragraph you say: "By December 1991, it was common knowledge throughout the region that refugees had become an element in ethnic competition." Can you tell us a bit about what you mean by that and perhaps amplify on that statement for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, aside from what I've already said which is that refugees from various ethnic groups were an obvious and logical product of warfare that was designed to draw clear borders between ethnic groups, we also have examples of ethnic -- excuse me, of refugees who are coerced to leave territory, even their own -- by their own side. For instance, we have examples of deals that were cut in the background perhaps which resulted in the creation of refugee problems where one might not have been in order to -- I don't know how to put it, trade populations to settle particular territorial dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, in the part of your report which I just referred you to, just a couple of lines down below the language I just quoted, you go on to say: "Refugees not being allowed to return even by members of their own ethnic group."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, we see two related phenomena, I suppose. There's -- there's the phenomenon of a particular government or military settling its own refugees on territory abandoned by others. So the refugee becomes a tool for establishing a claim to an area. We also have the occasional example of a given group moving its own people out of a territory that is considered insecure, perhaps, and moving them away. This is often as the result of a political side deal. I'm not sure if I'm making sense here, but it's a rather cynical process that we saw especially later on in the war in Bosnia but also in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In taking first of all the earlier time period again if I could ask you to look at Exhibit P 10273.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is an article in the Washington Post dated the 25th of November, 1991. It's again quite -- quite early, titled: "Serbia Begins Resettlement of Croatian Region; Displaced Serbs Moving into Abandoned Homes." Can you tell us again what that article is basically about and how that fits into the observations made in your paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the article describes -- describes two phenomena I suppose that work together. One is that there were plenty of Serbian refugees from -- from other parts of the -- of the region at war, and Serbia had also conquered territory and driven Croatian families, refugees, off of the land. And so the Serbs were simply settled in previously Croatian homes. In this case it's describing that process in the Eastern Slavonian Osijek region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just as a further example of that if in the text of this particular article before moving on, if you look -- and looking at the English version, page 2, the third paragraph on page 2. It says in connection with what you've said in your report it says, "Resettlement of occupied land is emerging as a fundamental tactic of the Serbian war effort against Croatia whose secession from the six Republic Yugoslav Federation in June prompted outrage among its large Serb minority and sparked the bloody war. Serbia, which is openly backed heavily armed Serb insurgents in Croatia, said it has no intention of allowing tens of thousands of displaced Croats and ethnic Hungarians to return to their Baranja, forgive me if I mispronounce that, homes, and force out Serbs such as Dusan Tulem." Again, that is part of the -- phenomena which the one -- you're saying one group would then move -- once the people were displaced they would move their own people or refugees into that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the ground this is why all the wars were fought. I mean, this is -- this isn't just part of a specific phenomenon. This is actually what was driving much of the military action. There were other -- other aspects to it of course but, yeah, this is exactly what I'm describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you next to go to Exhibit - excuse me - 10243. I think that -- well, I think it will still be in the small binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Right. I have it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a letter from a Catholic church official in Sarajevo, Puljic, to Franjo Tudjman, the president of Croatia on the 31st of October, 1993. And I'd like to direct your attention, please, to the third paragraph on that page which starts with the words "a commander in a municipality in Central Bosnia." Could you just read that paragraph to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you would find that account consistent with what you saw more generally and for example the earlier article from 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would call this -- an example of a much more cynical, I mean, what was already a cynical situation and cynical phenomenon. Here we have a Croat reporting back to Monsignor Puljic that he has been tasked with provoking the Muslim side to drive the Croats, his people, in other words, out of a particular area as part of a deal by which other territory would be given to the Croats. So this is obviously an escalation of the process but still, sure, it's part of the same continuum, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. On page -- going on to page 9 of your report, bottom of page 9, and carrying over to page 10 you have the statement: "Journalist and politicians widely and publicly discussed the likelihood that such intercommunal violence would engulf the Croatian communities of Bosnia and well. The partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina remains a particularly divisive issue among Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia." Now, I can probably tell you, Dr. Miller, that the Chamber has heard quite a bit about conflict and these issues being divisive between Croats and the Muslims for example. But can you say a bit more about why was this issue also divisive among Croats themselves? That is within the same ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I say a couple of reasons come to mind. One is that there were actually Croats who probably sincerely supported the unity of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia as well as in Bosnia, but also within Bosnia there were different populations of Croats that were separated in space and also separated I would say by -- by history, you know, the Croatian population of Herzegovina was probably guided by a set of interests that weren't always the same as the interests of the Croatian population of Central Bosnia or the Posavina region to the north, and so you know, I suppose that we like to think or perhaps they like to think that ethnic groups think monolithcally but that's, of course, never actually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard if I can turn your attention to Exhibits -- well, first of all P 0 -- excuse me, P 10241.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this appears to be another letter from a Catholic church official Andjelovic dated the 25th of September, 1993. In light of what you just said about there being different views even within you might say among the Croats living in the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would like you to look at paragraphs 1 and 2 of that -- numbered 1 and 2 of that letter and just if you can tell the Judges, does that illustrate the point or some of the points you made in your paper and in fact you just addressed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it illustrates the basic point which is that -- which is that events which had come before foretold in -- in the words of this gentleman, killings, ethnic cleansings, rapes and other types of violence. So again this is just an example of somebody whom I presume was reading the press that I was looking at and probably also witnessing a lot of this. In item number 2 he says, "This division is a historic catastrophe for Bosnian Croats because it means a final disappearance from Bosnia." I believe that he's writing as a Bosnian rather than a Herzegovinian Croat as its title implies and that he fears that what's happening in Bosnia is going to abandon let's say the central Bosnian Croatian population to their own devices. So again a more specific variation on the phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask you next to look at Exhibit P 10242.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe if I'm not mistaken this is another letter from the same Mr. Puljic or, excuse me, Monsignor Puljic that we looked at a few moments ago, this one dated the 11th of February, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this again just for the record is referenced or addressed to Franjo Tudjman, president of Croatia. If I can ask you to look at paragraphs numbered 2 and 3 on the second page. Just ask you the same questions or similar questions to the ones I asked you a few moments ago, how -- how does what is written in paragraph -- on paragraphs 2 and 3 relate to the observations you made in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to quickly scan paragraph 3 if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Puljic is turning to Tudjman obviously in Croatia, not in Bosnia, in an appeal to not pursue policies that would contribute to division between the Croatian populations of Herceg-Bosna and the rest of the Croats of Bosnia. I believe the -- the underlying theme here is that he fears that the Tudjman government is supporting Herceg-Bosna and is betraying some willingness to abandon the Croatian populations in Bosnia outside of Herceg-Bosna again to their own devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just in paragraph 3 before moving on, when you talk about these other Muslims outside of Herceg-Bosna, Monsignor Puljic makes reference to, he says: "Conflicts and insufficient tactfulness towards Muslims bring 40 per cent of BiH Croats who will stay out of envisaged Croatian units in a difficult position." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess that's a specific example to which referring to. Insufficient tactfulness I suppose means potentially aggressive or actually aggressive actions towards Muslims in those regions in which Croats are not a majority is -- so in other words, I would extrapolate that the authorities in Herceg-Bosna are doing things once again that are going to result in hostility from the Muslim population towards the Croats of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, beginning to finish up on your first report we've focused primarily or often so far on the local and regional media on papers such as Danas and Vreme. Did you also look, however, at more of the international press and what was being also being reported in international organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think just by way of a quick review you can see that starting on about page 16 of your report and following particularly you talk about the Mazowiecki reports and various UN Resolutions and reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mazowiecki starts on 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And just in finishing up this first report, then, if I could direct your attention to the top of page 19. You make the statement although -- it's actually above what you then -- the section -- the title conclusions, it seems to me is a fair summary of what you've said in the previous 18 pages. "Thus by mid-1992, a pattern of violence purposely focused on civilians as a means of compelling them to abandon a given territory had emerged and was widely reported and known locally, regionally, and internationally." Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a nutshell, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you do appear to make on the very last page of your report, paragraph 20, you do appear to make some exception or put one type of conduct, I'll put it that way for now, as distinct from some of the others you've mentioned, and I believe you say that it might not have been -- if I can characterise it this way: By mid-1992, it might not have been forecast to what extent rape or sexual assault might have become a feature of the conflict. Is that a fair reading of what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You can see from the report that there are actual examples of reports of a pattern of rape, but most of them are framed speculatively and so I guess I'm just demonstrating an excess of caution here, perhaps, but I don't think that rape or sexual violence rises to the same level of obviousness as other phenomena described in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Up until the point of the middle of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my questions on the first of the two reports, and it might be a time for a break or if there are particular questions the Chamber might have on the first report it might also be a time for that or we can have the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now have a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Scott, and studying the second report, I would have a follow-up question to ask, Witness. We have seen that you have researched in particular in the American press. So there are two articles, two stories of the Washington Post and of the San Francisco Chronicle, but in your research in your university where you teach, did you also study the European press, European newspapers. At the time the European press, had it also reported a certain number of things which were happening on the ground? Did you yourself research anything in the British press or in the French press or anything else, Swiss press, for instance, in stories which were drafted in 1991 or 1992 on this phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't make a study of the European press part of this, no. But I have read the European press in the past, and I don't think its coverage differs much from the US press in that regard. If anything, it was more in-depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. Did you look at agency dispatchers at the time, Reuters, AFP, or other world news agencies which were supposed normally to report on what was happening? Have you studied these reports or news from the news agencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a -- not -- not specifically. I mean, I have an enormous stack of material that didn't make its way into this report that includes wire reports. I actually chose to use signed articles because I view them as more credible on that basis, but -- so, yes, but I didn't include them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very last question: The State Department declassified certain documents, probably concerning this period. Have you yourself consulted such documents in the department of state to know what were the interesting or relevant documents which would have given an account of the events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't, but I actually don't personally think that State Department dispatches addresses the question that I was addressing. I mean, a state department dispatch that has recently been open to the public is not going to be something that reflects for the public in 1991 and 1992 what was going on. I mean, I very purposely stuck as much as possible to the widely available open-source materials because the question was how much would people have known was going on at the time. But I also haven't looked at the state department dispatches even for any other purpose. Frankly, I'm not sure that we can take it for granted that anything from the state department has been declassified at this point, maybe, but that's just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and just to follow up on something the president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- asked you about. You just mentioned and perhaps I should have asked you myself, the material that is footnoted in your report, is it fair to say that it does not exhaust -- or does not indicate or reflect an exhaustive listing of all the material that you consider in the course of preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not exhaustive at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour if that is the case, then we do need an exhaustive list because we're at a disadvantage. How am I to know what this gentleman looked at. That was one of the things I was going to be asking the gentlemen. Did he prepare a list of what he considered, what he did not consider so that we at least know. Now we know that he says there is an exhaustive list. Where is the list? What did you consult, sir? Provide that to us. I would ask that it be provided to us before the cross-examination be conducted. We're at a distinct disadvantage if we're going to be shooting in the dark at this point. This gentleman is supposed to a Ph.D. from a fine university. I'm relying on his footnotes. His footnotes are second and third sources. Now he's saying that he considered other stuff. Where is that other stuff?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might briefly respond, please. I think that the state of affairs is this: I think that the witness quite properly responded to your question, Mr. President, on various other media sources that in the course of preparing a report he would have looked at more material that in fact is reflected in the footnotes to his report. Frankly I don't think that comes as much of a surprise. I don't think anyone would -- I wouldn't have thought anyone conducting a report of this nature would list everything they possibly looked at over the weeks or months that they conducted their research. The bottom line and clearly what the Chamber will have to decide is not what other material was or was not considered, but whether the material as reflected in the report and as supported by the witness in his testimony and has explained, the Court considers that to have provided probative value to the Court and not how many other documents may or may not have been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just -- if I could just bring to the Trial Chamber's attention we had one particular witness. He was an expert as well. He was on sniping. He was rather different. And I made the point of pointing out that in that particular instance the gentleman had been provided with a letter or a memorandum where he was asked specifically what his tasks would be. The letter listed what information he was to look at and also there was a caveat towards the end indicating that if there was anything else that he needed to consult as an expert to do so and keep track of it, and I made a point of noting it on the record because I wanted to bring it to the Trial Chamber's attention because that is generally the way things are done with expert witnesses. Something that wasn't done with, say, Mr. Donia, and we went through that route with Mr. Donia as to what exactly he was provided. Granted the Prosecution in this instance it would appear simply asked the gentleman to answer one particular question, and then left it up to the gentleman to decide what sources he would look at, what sources he would consider in order to answer that particular question. That's fine. What I'm saying, however, is this: If I am to cross-examine and confront this witness based on some of the conclusions that he's reached, I'm entitled to know exactly what he looked at, what was available to him, what he looked at, what he considered, what he did not consider, and from there to go on. But at this point all I have are the footnotes. So I'm going -- I'm under the impression at least that when he's making an assertion we see that he cites a particular source. In one instance he cited a book, a textbook. I believe it was this book over here by Mr. Burg and Mr. Shoup, and when you go to it it's a footnote citing an another text. So he's citing a text that cites another text. Of course we don't see that. But at least there there's some sort of transparency. So we know exactly. So I can, you know, I know whether he's actually relying on first-hand, second-hand, third-hand. So I'm entitled to know exactly what the gentleman did. Now, I can handle this on cross-examination, and I'm perfectly willing to do so. However, before I go into any substantive cross-examination, I do believe based on the representations made by the gentleman that I'm entitled to everything, to at least the list of everything that he considered, because there maybe something that he should have considered but did not consider and that also goes to confrontation. And I believe my colleague, Mr. Murphy, wished to chime in on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to add one brief point. I think the force of Mr. Karnavas's point lies in this really, that the witness has been called to deal with the state of public knowledge or public opinion, and since that is the expressed goal of his paper, it is really relevant to know the extent of the published literature and publications that he looked at because otherwise we don't know what potentially the state of public opinion was. I think Mr. Karnavas is right for that reason alone. I think if a student in one of the witness's classes had submitted the paper in that state it probably would rate a B minus but not very much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Witness, the observations of the Defence could have been integrated in cross-examination, but independently from that inasmuch as myself I have asked a few questions asking you what you relied on to do your study. It seems that in your first report this is a series of references with their footnotes, and I suppose that the conclusions of your report are supported by the documents which are mentioned in the footnotes, but off-the-cuff from memory you said so, you admitted there are other documents, other stuff which you studied to -- in order to analyse the question of the expertise you had to conduct. Could you tell us, just by memory, if it's not asking too much, what were the other documents or sources to which you referred and which you did not mention in footnotes so that Defence may know exactly what you have read and studied if it's possible. If not, you just tell us. Tell me that you can't and you have only quoted the main books, texts. So can you complement what you've seen or read or what are the databases, newspapers you have used for your study, what documents and so on? Would you be in a position to give a complete list of what you have actually used for both reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I responded to Mr. Scott that this was only part of what I could have used, what I meant was that out of the sources I did look at, there were many more articles that I could have used as examples; meaning from Danas, from Vreme, from the various western press organisations that I used. You know, philosophically I'm not used to court practice, but I do know as an historian when I do something or when any historian does his work or her work, we actually presume that they've done their work faithfully, and that what they've produced is a representation of what they actually saw. So in other words, I don't think that -- you know, what I've done is tried to capture the essence of the public -- public knowledge through these various press organs at the time. What I've looked at, I mean, I don't really know what you mean. If you mean can I give you a list of all the articles that I've read? At this point I can't do that. But I can tell you that, you know, what I drew from is represented in the footnotes to this paper and that there was nothing, for instance, that would act to somehow mitigate the conclusion. I think it's fairly impossible to -- I can't imagine that there's some sources out there that I didn't look at that would have somehow mitigated the impression that it was general knowledge that the type of warfare that was being waged was in fact being waged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to make some headway, it seems that you have examined newspapers of ex-Yugoslavia. You mentioned two, Danas and Vreme. And have you also read other weeklies or daily newspapers in -- of ex-Yugoslavia, except Danas and Vreme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I looked at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Danas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I looked a bit at Nin, which is a Serbian weekly, and at a Croatian weekly that was called Hrvatski Tjednik. In both cases I considered and I think most people who are familiar with this field would agree that those two weekly magazines were in 1991 and 1992 unreliable, and in this case they were more likely to provide more horrifying accounts of warfare than the other two, and I kept them out of my report because I don't think they're reliable, but they're unreliable to -- you know, in the direction of making things seem worse than they were. If the Serbian or Croatian public were relying on them I think the picture they received would be even more extreme than the one I've proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this precision. Concerning the American press by memory, what did you consult as daily newspapers or weeklies of the American press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually consulted the American press less overall than I did the Yugoslav press because I felt that the Yugoslav press was more likely to be giving a picture to the people of Yugoslavia but, nonetheless, I looked at the Washington Post, The New York Times, the San Francisco Chronicle, the St. Louis post dispatch, I believe, Chicago Tribune, Los Angeles Times. I'm not sure if all of them wound up in my footnotes or not but those were all -- well, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. In the footnotes there are several books which you quote. Are there any which are specifically important or of a medium importance and which you didn't quote? Would you remember any now? Could you tell us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Books that I've consulted? You know, I consult books as a way of -- as a way of life, and so, you know, using the Burg-Shoup book for instance, it's just a book that's part of what I do. There are other books that I mention, actually, in the report by people like Andrew Wachtel, Sabrina Ramet and others, again is only a fraction of the books that I make my living using, frankly. So again I guess to produce some type of list of the books that I consulted would be difficult and extraordinarily time-consuming.
