With the exception off the top of my head of the Burg book and a book by a person named Sumantra Bose dealing with Mostar, those would be the only two books that I specifically consulted in the process of doing these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you've finished I'd like to seek clarification regarding the record on page 45, lines 17 and 18 in response to your question, the witness says that he followed the Yugoslav press because he considered that the Yugoslav press would give a better picture to the people of Yugoslavia, et cetera. Now, since the term Yugoslavia until 1991 referred to one entity and after 1991 some people colloquially speaking who weren't well educated incorporated here the independent republics which stepped down from Yugoslavia, perhaps that could be clarified. Did he follow one press, the Yugoslav press, up until the independence of these states or did he follow the press in the other republics after independence except for the two that he mentioned, two periodicals he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard the question. When you speak of Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia disintegrated and there were several republics which came into being. So when you speak of the Yugoslav press, are you mentioning newspapers of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and so on or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've mentioned the four that I looked at, and I apologise for colloquially using the term Yugoslav when I should have said Serbian and Croatian. Vreme, Danas, Nin, and Tjednik, were the four formerly Yugoslav press organs that I consulted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Scott, let's now proceed and try and make some headway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, as I indicated before the break we've completed the direct examination on the first of your reports unless -- unless something were to come up, perhaps supplemental, but I would like to turn now to the second report which again we indicated earlier was Exhibit P 10240, titled the Persistence of Herceg-Bosna After the Washington Agreement and Dayton. And just as I did with the first report, if I might just by way of introduction would it be a fair -- would I fairly state the question that was put to you if I indicated that you were asked to research and present information indicating whether an entity known as Herceg-Bosna, first as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Chamber's heard, established in November 1991, and then what became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in August 1993, but I'll just refer to those as Herceg-Bosna. Did you research and then prepare a report on whether Herceg-Bosna continued to exist and operate after the Washington and Dayton Agreements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that is the report that we're obviously looking at now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In footnote 1 of your report you make reference, we're back to again to the media we were talking about to some degree, and you referred to a New York Times article. Could I ask you please to look at Exhibit P 10278.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that, on the bottom of the article, it says after introductory a couple of words it says: "Put simply, the Bosnian Croats, like Bosnian Serbs, still want part of Bosnia for themselves. For these Croats, Western Mostar is the capital of their designated state of Herceg-Bosna and is central to their vision of a Greater Croatia." And on the last page of that article, before I put a couple of questions to you, in the fourth -- excuse me, I believe the fifth paragraph on that page 4 it says after the -- excuse me, after the first sentence of that paragraph: "But it is hard in Mostar to escape the conclusion that the Croats of Herceg-Bosna are working for a Greater Croatia." Now, I just point out those to you as -- as an introduction to your paper. What did you find generally? What did the literature indicate to you about the continued existence and operation of Herceg-Bosna after Washington and Dayton? Perhaps you could just give us an overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before that can we know what literature we're talking about? What is the literature? I'm not talking about Roger Cohen who is writing -- who is a famous journalist who writes opinions for the news papers. I'm asking exactly what literature is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again Dr. Miller have you relied principally on the materials that is cited in the footnotes to your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you could state by way then of overview what your research showed in terms of the continued existence and operation of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My research shows that the government of Herceg-Bosna, even following the Washington Agreement and the Dayton peace agreement, the collective members of that government, Croatian leaders of that region, have been very reluctant to see the structures of that government disappear. In other words, it persists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the -- at the end of the first paragraph of your report in fact you quote an article, quoting one of the accused in this case, Mr. Prlic, and at the end of that paragraph it says this is in your report now page 1: "According to the president of Herceg-Bosna at the time the Washington Agreement was negotiated, Jadranko Prlic, speaking in February 1995, Croats 'had no interest in a unitary government in Bosnia and are only interested in federal institutions and confederation with Croatia.'" And is it correct that you took that from the Roger Cohen article that we were just looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just for the record can we find that the next to last paragraph on page 2 of the news article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just so the record is very precise, the quoted language, and I'm quoting Mr. Cohen's article, Mr. Prlic was described as the president of Herceg-Bosna. Were you aware that he was the prime minister of Herceg-Bosna in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The term is "Predsednik Vlade," "prime minister." President of the government, I suppose, literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of your report and other places as well, you refer to a man named Ante Jelavic whose name may have come up in these proceedings so far but perhaps not any particular way. Could you just say briefly what you understood Mr. Jelavic's role to be during the conflict in question and focusing on the period 1992 to 1994? What did you understand his position or role to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the war he was in charge of or assistant to the person in charge of procurement. He was the head -- excuse me. Which meant that he played a very important role in bringing war materials and other important things into Herceg-Bosna primarily from Croatia. He was a supply officer, I suppose, on a much higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, just so there's not a misunderstanding, a supply officer could mean a number of things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What rank or position did you understand Mr. Jelavic to be operating at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rank in the military?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I don't recall his rank in the military, but he was assistant to the person who was the head of procurement, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at Exhibit P 10279. And can you just tell us is this one of the documents that you referred to and in light of the question of what documents you referred to is this one of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again just to be -- in light of the questions that have been raised, I'd like to point you specifically to a couple of examples. Could I ask you, if you go to page 1 of the report. Not the preface page -- prefatory pages that are marked with small Roman numerals, but if you go to the first page of the actual text under the section introduction. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And toward the bottom of that page there is the language, there is the paragraph that says: "Since 1994, the HDZ leadership in cooperation with HVIDR-A (Croatian war veterans and invalids association and power for Herzegovina economic interest) has repeatedly blocked not only internationally community efforts to reunite Mostar but also the implementation of the federation agreement and the Dayton Peace Agreement." Is that what you cite in, for example, footnote 2 of your -- of this, the second report? You can verify that if you wish by looking at your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go to - and I'm not going to take you through all the passages in that report that you've looked -- that you've cited but others may - but let me next ask you to look at Exhibit 10280. And this is a document that is titled -- well, it was apparently produced by the European stability initiative and it's the title of this document is "Reshaping international priorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the end of the Nationalist Regimes and the Future of the Bosnian State 22 March 2001." Is that another of the documents that you relied upon in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again by way of example, if I can ask you to go to page 9 of that document, of the exhibit. And if I can direct your attention, for example, to paragraph number 3 on that page. When you -- the language at the end of that paragraph which says "The Croat national Congress voted to withdraw from the federation constitutional structure until such time as full constitutional and genuine equality of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina is provided." And do you cite that in footnote 14 of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again I won't go through all the other passages, but can I next ask you to look at Exhibit P 10281. This is another report put out by the International Crisis Group. Their report number 39, it says, 13th of August, 1998, titled "Changing course. Implications of the divide in Bosnian Croat politics." Again, is that one of the documents you relied on for purposes of preparing your second report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In page -- on page 2 of your report, the end of the paragraph beginning on that page you make the statement that as late as August 1999, "The Croat side does not support a unified army in BiH because they did not want to create another mini former JNA, et cetera." Can you tell us just in general - and we'll show you a couple of documents in a moment - but what did you see in the context of researching this report as to whether the role of Herceg-Bosna if you will, and whether there was a general effort to combine what was the HVO into the national or the army of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Strike the word national and say the federation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the consensus of the sources that I consulted would be that the HVO -- excuse me, the government of the Herceg-Bosna -- the Croats of Herzegovina, I suppose at this point, did not want to see the HVO totally dissolved. Perhaps -- apparently dissolved while maintaining structures that existed before in order to sustain them under cover, if you will, but I think the general sentiment is that they did not want the HVO to be totally subsumed by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please in that regard to look at Exhibit P 01267.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, it's a rather long and complex document, but can you give us an overview -- I'll point you to a couple of passages but perhaps while I'm looking for that you could -- can you give us any sort of overview of the -- what this document says and, if you will, bottom line in terms of the integration of the HVO into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Well, this is a document produced by the -- by Ante Jelavic in 1998, and the general sense of the document is that the -- the -- the HVO or the Croatian army at this point should not be allowed to be totally subsumed by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina again. It's sort of a page by page example of the fact that this -- that the Croats did not -- did not wish to see the HVO disappear. Aligning -- aligning the interests of the HVO with the army of the Republic of Croatia, for instance, as opposed to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you in a particular as an example to go to page 16 of this document, the exhibit. In paragraph number 4 on that page and this particular item is referring to integration of the armed forces but at levels both either above the corps level or below the corps level, and in the second half of that paragraph they're talking about integration below the corps level of organisation, and if I can ask you at the -- toward the end of that paragraph does it say: "At no cost will we ever allow this. For the total merger into a single army other qualities would slowly be lost which characterise us as member of the Croatian people otherwise it leads us to the creation of some kind of a'Bosniak nation.'"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- it reflects a generalised fear I suppose among Croats of that region and the HVO leadership that allowing their military to be merged with that of Bosnia and Herzegovina would eventually sort of institutionally contribute to the disappearance of Croats themselves in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could my colleague clarify with the witness something? There's either a technical mistake or a mistake in the transcript, but I seem to feel that he said P [Realtime transcript read in error"1267"] 10267, that the document was signed by Ante Jelavic, although this does not follow from the document. So I'm not quite clear on this. Perhaps the document is a compilation of a number of documents and one of the documents and the only one which in fact has a signature was signed by General -- Colonel-General Stanko Sopta, and that is addressed to Ante Jelavic. So what is in the transcript does not correspond to what we have in the document. So there's no point in clarifying this during the cross-examination. It would be a better idea to clarify it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, there is a mistake. It's 10267. And indeed there are about two documents. One has 18 pages and after that there is a letter sent to Ante Jelavic on 29 June 1998. And then there is -- there are also other letters sent to Miljenko Delic, 26 June 1998. And then other pieces of correspondence, letters. So maybe we could sort of clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I think that the Court's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend but for the record once again yes you provided the correct number of the document. It is 10267, 10267. That's what I'm speaking about. The first 18 documents and the tables attached I think belong to that document, although that is guesswork too, and that wasn't signed by anyone. So we actually don't know what that document is at all. And then we have the two letters that are signed and are indeed addressed to Jelavic. But to put them all in that same basket and say that is a document from Ante Jelavic I don't think that has any grounds at all. So perhaps it would be a good idea if you could tell us the source. We see that the document was procured from the Croatian archives by the OTP. So did the OTP provide the witness with it, the expert witness, or did the expert witness get it himself from the archives in view of the fact that in early 2000 the Croatian archives said that any physical person who could have had -- who could show proof of scientific interest could have had access to the papers. Now, papers compiled by Croats in Bosnia up 1993, as far as I'm concerned, have never seen them, so I'm not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can attempt to clarify and then I'll let the witness certainly speak for himself in terms of -- he may be able to correct himself on the signature, but to answer counsel's question, you'll notice on the first page that there is in fact a stamp of the Croatian state archives which the Chamber has probably -- has seen before. This is a bit of a different format than usual but indicates on the front page they may have changed their stamp more recently. But it comes from the archive. This particular collection came from documents that had existed at the office of the president, and on the -- I'm looking now on the translation for those working in English. On the front page it indicates stamped for receipt, Republic of Croatia, office of the president of the republic, 22 October 1998. It's -- Your Honour, it's simply the -- this is the form which the document came that was provided by the archive. We didn't combine them in any way. At the time the document was found it existed in this compilation, and we simply took the document as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, you might want to -- in light of questions that have been raised, you might want to look at the document and you may, if you feel, want to correct yourself whether which parts are signed by various persons. If you might be allowed to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, obviously I erred. The whole document was not authored by Ante Jelavic, and that's about -- that's about the extent of my explanation. I understood that it was presented to Ante Jelavic, but that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just a couple of other examples --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that my colleague is moving on. This is quite obviously a relevant question, whether the expert witness came by this report -- this document when he wrote his report and used it as a source or whether he was provided it by the Prosecution, because what my learned friend just asked him, I gather that he got it from the archives. Now, who took it out from the archive? And I think that this is a relevant question because these are two different situations. So I request that the Prosecutor ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the -- did you receive the document from the archives or did the Prosecution give it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received it from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I asked -- yes, Your Honour. I was about to say that. In the process of reviewing documents and as the Chamber will recall, the Chamber is constantly encouraging us to put as many documents to witnesses as possible. When we saw this document which was obtained fairly recently, which we then felt possibly related to what the witness had addressed in his report, it was shown to the witness for the purposes of asking him exactly that. "If you had seen this document or showing you this document, how did that fit into the observations made in your report?" And that's what I've asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission. In view of the fact that we have here a witness who is an expert, and we received his expert opinion, his expert report which we received at the end of June, and along with the document already at that time we had the footnotes, and when we read, all of us, the expert report, we read the footnotes, too, and we read the literature which we considered to be important, that could be found if public records. And the Prosecution said that it was not duty-bound to disclose all the sources because they are publicly accessible material, and most of the material which the expert witness quotes in his footnotes we were able to come by, that's true. Then the OTP over the past two or three weeks before the witness came in, out of courtesy I assume, really did provide us with all the material from the footnotes, all the material on the basis of which the expert witness founds his expert report, along with a number of other documents too. Now, is the position this: Is the OTP saying that after the witness wrote his report and statement that there are indeed other documents which confirm what the witness, the expert witness, has said? Now, the witness wrote what he thinks and what he said, and he told us the sources on the basis of which this was done and he filed it. So I see no reason why we should expand the circle of information that we received there the expert witness, especially not the circle of sources. And if I might warn the Trial Chamber of the following: This document that we're discussing now, a question that we're talking about due diligence here, it says due diligence, because the Prosecution -- the material that came from the presidential office into the archive, and we've just heard that they were documents from the presidential office, they arrived in the archives in 2005, and they were not disclosed to us. And the Prosecution hasn't seen them either. It was only in 2007, and that's what they say when they ask for the introduction of the presidential documents, it was only in 2007 in reviewing documents from the Croatian archive which arrived there from the presidential office and in connection with another trial at this Tribunal, the Gotovina trial, found that there were indeed interesting documents in those piles and piles of documents which have to do with this case too. And now in a submission they ask that they be subsequently introduced. Now, nothing was done for two years, and then two years later they say, Ha, we have new documents. That is not due diligence. And then furthermore he provides this expert witness with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, I understand quite quickly what one is trying to say. Mr. Scott, your colleague is apparently saying that some of the documents that we have before us, in particular 10267, suggesting that you have had this document for a certain time already but have not disclosed it or had not disclosed it to the Defence during that time and that recently; namely, in the context of the Gotovina case, you realised, discovered, that those documents could be of interest in this case. Is that true or not? What do you have to say on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is basically correct, Your Honour, and that's what I was wanting to try to explain further and just so there is no misunderstanding. We've been -- I think it's sometimes an overused word, entirely transparent about that at least in two ways; that is, one as is normally, the case we provided a list of potential or proposed preliminary exhibits to all the Defence teams two weeks ago in which this document and others were listed. So it's not a surprise today but consistent with past practice a number of documents were put on that list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why was this document not disclosed initially to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It has -- it has been disclosed Your Honour, and that's why I said we were transparent in two ways. I told you one and now I'll tell you the second one; and that is that we filed a motion seeking the addition of I think something like 26 or 28 new documents obtained from the office of the president for the reasons stated therein, and I can tell the Chamber that the Office of the Prosecutor for years, for literally years, into at least 2000 and actually well before that, have tried to collect as much relevant documentation from the government of Croatia as possible and has made many trips to the archive. However, over the years, in our experience, various materials have been added to the archive as the years have gone by and materials that were there in 2005 or 2007 might not have been there in 2000 and 2001. In the context of an admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me quote a particular example that is not in the English translation because I'm working more and more from the B/C/S version because it makes it possible to discover interesting things. For example, in 562, that in B/C/S is the last page, 562061111562, it's not very well written, I note the following: Apparently when the army of the federation was set up, the elements of the HVO and the ABiH were included, and I note, I find this somewhat odd, that with regard to the tanks we note that the M-60, the HVO had 22 and the ABiH 23, the MX-30 HVO had 10 and the ABiH 40, the T-55 the HVO had 7 and the ABiH 14 and so on and so forth. Whereas in other evidence we've spoken of tanks and helicopters, because here we see helicopters as well that are listed. We also have the number of helicopters, Bell UH-1H. There were 15, five for the HVO and 10 for the ABiH. So your a military analyst, because apparently according to what I've read in a number works the OTP has military analysts. So your military analyst must have realised and been aware of the content of this page. And if this was not disclosed to the Defence then it should have been. So you recognise to some extent that it's only very recently that you discovered the importance of these documents and that you filed the motion for the admission of new documents. Is that what you're saying Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President,. I certainly can't get into the number of tanks that have been allocated to various sides. I would note that this, however this information, at least as I see it at quick -- on a very quick glance relates to states of affairs in 1998, not 1993, but let me be very clear and I'm sorry if I have not been clear so far, this document was first received from Zagreb on about the 27th of June this year. 27th of June, 2007. As we say in our motion, the related motion that I referred to a few moments ago, as soon as the documents were processed and identified we -- they were disclosed and have been disclosed to the Defence I think at the earliest possible opportunity. The Chamber will understand that when documents come in to the building they have to be processed. They're given numbers. They have been translated. They have to be some idea or at least a cursory, someone looks at them for the purposes of what they are. It does take some days. It doesn't come in one hour and go out the next. The fact of the matter is that this document was first collected on the 20 -- or received on the 27th of year and then disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might, a correction for the record. There seems to be a misunderstanding, maybe through the interpretation or translation. I'm not challenging the fact or objecting to the fact that the Prosecution disclosed this document or others or -- or found the documents two or three weeks ago and that they are documents which the Prosecution obtained in June 2007. Quite the contrary. I give them full recognition. From June to September they dealt with that very quickly so that's not something that I'm criticising or objecting to. However, the Prosecution in the spring of 2005 was informed from the office of coordination in the Croatian government for cooperation with the ICTY, informed the -- the Defence because we had a request there, we wanted to obtain some presidential documents as well, I don't have the letter now to show you, but we were informed that all the documents which the presidential office was ready to make public were transferred to the national archive, and we were told, "Gentlemen," and this was equally said to the Prosecution and the Defence, "you can go to the national archive, you're free to go and look for the documents that you need." And I just have to give you a bit of history here, Your Honours. This happened previously, from the beginning of 1990 -- 2002, in fact, when all the HVO documents which reached Croatia by one channel or another were also placed in the archive and everybody went there, both the Defence and the Prosecution. So my thesis is this: The Prosecution from the spring of 2005 was informed by the government and the presidential office that the documents for which the Prosecution was interested in based on the descriptions sent out were to be found in the archive. So they say, "Gentlemen, go to the archive and you can find them and take them." Despite that information the Prosecution did not go to the archive because it decided not to spend its resources on that and not to go to the archive and it was only in 2005 as my colleague said a moment ago, 2007, I meant to say, 2007, when they received a large package of documents which the investigators of the OTP took from the archive, and they looked for documents for the Gotovina trial, and then they came across other documents as well. It was only in June 2007 as my colleague said that they did disclose them to us very quickly, and I commend them for that. However, for two years they undertook nothing at all. So where is due diligence there, I ask you. I don't think it's fair that after two years of sleeping on it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, do you have a response and then will move on. Mr. Kovacic is saying that you were not diligent enough since as early as 2005 you could have had these documents, whereas, in fact you only had them in your possession in June 2007. So we can say that you didn't really take off as quickly as you could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope the Chamber -- my apology. Your Honour, I hope the Chamber knows by now that I try not to engage in overstatement or make promises that I can't keep or statements that I can't support. I certainly can't know what we might have found if we'd made another two or three trips between 2005 and 2007 to the archive. I do know that the Office of the Prosecutor has gone to the archive many, many occasions since these documents -- various parts of these documents first became available in 2000. It's like going into a large library, Your Honour. I suppose if one walked into -- I hate -- I'm sorry to use an American example, but if one walked into the Library of Congress and said, you're now charged with everything in here, you're now on notice and are responsible for knowing everything that's on the -- how many floors of the building and how many stacks of documents, and now you're going to be held responsible for what's in the building, I'm not sure that's really a fair way to proceed. We're talking about hundreds of thousands of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I know the Library of Congress. I've actually been there. But if you ask someone where to find something, you will be given guidance. So I imagine when you go to the Croatian archives, and you say these are the documents I would need, for example, documents regarding the HVO and military aspects, someone will surely tell you this is where to find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think on that point, I think Mr. Kovacic would probably agree with me that the state organisation is certainly dramatically improved since 2000, but it's still -- it can be a hit or miss project again, as you can understand, that documents have been collected from various sources that might not have been exactly filed in the most appropriate folder at the time. I know from working very closely with the people who have conducted various of these missions, that while they have I think exercised great diligence trying to locate as many relevant documents as possible, these -- this particular document and several -- a number of others had never been seen prior to June of 2007. Your Honour, I have to leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has taken good note of what Mr. Kovacic said and we'll rule on this issue later. I think it's best for you to continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I have also looked at this document before this morning. It has no signature, no indication of the author. It has no date. It has no addressee. One does not know to whom it was destined. I -- I fear this is a bit -- a paper which may be interested for the contents but it's hanging in the air, and it would be really helpful if it could be tied down to earth in some way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going through it now, and I think that that is -- I also don't want to get bogged down frankly in this one particular document, but if I could have one more minute -- I think there are a number of signatures in the document, if I recall. I think the first part of the document -- I think the first part of the document was apparently prepared at least under the guidance of someone named -- an officer named -- sorry, I just lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I was only talking about the 18 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ah, the first 18 pages. Yes, Your Honour. I think that you're absolutely right. In the English translation it doesn't indicate that, but I'm looking at the briefs of the Croatian original. I think you're right, Your Honour. I'm looking at ERN page 06110552, which appears to be -- I -- your point is taken, Your Honour, and on that one I see that there are other names associated in the document, but again I hate to take the -- Stanko Sopta on one of them, Mr. Jelavic on another one, Miroslav Grubesic on another one, but I agree on the first 18 pages there doesn't seem to be a name. Your Honour, it answers the questions raised and I don't think it's -- and I don't think it's an absolutely essential document to the gentleman's analysis and again it wasn't, but I think not to belabour this too much longer, it wasn't included in his report but was presented to him as a document subsequently found that he might -- he might be able to comment on in the context of his report. So in any event, it was not a document that relied on in reaching the conclusions in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Having taken all the time to do that, if I could ask you to Exhibit P 10282.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm turning now to the latter part of your report, the second half roughly, I mean it's a short report but starting around page 4 and continue on about various developments concerning Mr. Jelavic and then later on in page -- starting on page 6 is when you include in your report the language that we quoted from a few minutes ago. The first paragraph on page 6. On 3 March 2001, the HDZ dominated the Croatian national assembly, the HNS, in Mostar, announced the formation of an illegal parallel Croat mini state in Bosnia combining two predominantly Croat populated cantons. The HNS sent an ultimatum to the international community saying the new "entity" would leave Bosnia in two weeks unless controversial changes to legislation governing election of deputies to the state parliament's Upper House were reversed. And when I ask to look at P 10282 is that one of the sources, and you see several in the ongoing footnotes, that you cited in connection with this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to also then go to Exhibit P 10283. And is that again an article -- well, let me ask you to look at that and also let me ask you to look at Exhibit P 10284. Perhaps we can talk about them together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you simply confirm that those are additional documents that you cite in your report in that part of the report about the developments concerning the removal of Mr. Jelavic in 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with the -- the conclusions or observations that you make in your second report, I would like then next to direct your attention to two final exhibits, and that -- the first of those is Exhibit 8448. And that -- those -- now, we may have reached a point where they will be in one of the other binders. I think binder number 2 for those who are working with the binders. Binder -- I'm told now binder 1. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the Judges in this case have heard before about -- or have seen a number of transcripts, records of conversations or meetings which we've come to refer to as presidential transcripts. This is one from the 2nd of September, 1994, and I would like you to please turn, if you will, to page 18 of that document, and it should be that those working in B/C/S should be able to find it also on page 18 of that version, but English page 18. Just in context this is a meeting involving a number of people, including Dario Kordic, President Tudjman, Mr. Susak, and at the bottom of that page Susak says: "Or if we allow the Muslims to somehow cut us off on Neretva." Then going on to page 19. Jadranko Prlic: "Their official stance is that Herceg-Bosna has never been stronger." Again I refer to this as March -- excuse me September 1994. "Herceg-Bosna has never been stronger because they consider that to be a sabotage on the part of the Croats towards. There are many implications in that respect. I even think that these two even today, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in its internal organisation is Herceg-Bosna and then what they were two months ago." President Tudjman intervenes and says, "Let's get this straight but formally. Do not point out the Croatian occupation. Keep it up and strengthen it in practice but go for the creation of the federation." And I would like to draw your attention to one other passage before I ask you questions about both of those. Can I ask you then next to go to page 38 of the same transcript. And again on page 38 you have first Mr. Kordic speaking, then the President Franjo Tudjman, and then Mr. Prlic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRLIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Mr. President, every Croat in Bosnia-Herzegovina is a paid Croat. Everyone is on the salary of the Herceg-Bosna budget except for that part that is in the Serbian territory. He is getting a salary as a soldier, a policeman, man who works in education, medicine, a hundred thousand people are supported by the Herceg-Bosna budget with pensions and everything together with everything else. There are not very many left without a salary. "President: All right, but it is a problem. The second problem that Dario has just mentioned. "Jadranko Prlic: This is the most important problem. They can have between three and five times better living conditions than the Muslims. This is the most important issue. "Susak: At the same time they're leaving. They have better living conditions somewhere else and they leave. "Tudjman: That is why you should be thinking about something else. Brajkovic told me that Muslims are already applying for dual citizenship." "Interruption." Tudjman continues: "There are no dilemmas here. Today they will receive a passport. Tomorrow they will have a glass of wine with you and eat meat. In 10 years they will be Croats of the Muslim persuasion. Do you understand?" Can you tell the Judges in terms of the discussion of Herceg-Bosna how that fits into your conclusions that Herceg-Bosna continued to exist and operate after Washington and Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If he could go on and read the rest of the portion of it, because apparently it's quite telling, because they don't -- because Mr. -- because President Tudjman talks about not having the Muslims go along with Alija's fundamentalism, and I think that becomes important because at this stage, remember, Iran is playing a role as well as other Mujahedins are playing a role in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there is quite a bit of fundamentalism being bandied about, even at this stage of the game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, would you read the rest of the sentence concerning Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. I'm happy to, Your Honour, I just don't know what it has too do with the continued existence of Herceg-Bosna but I'm happy to do so. "I have said this to my own and to you, we have to be indulgent here regardless of the reason they do it for today. In that way we can take them out of their formations. At least they will not go along with Alija's fundamentalism. Apart from that, there will always be some people doing it for whatever reasons." And I think, Dr. Miller, I put the question to you before the interruption which hasn't yet been answered, and I'll just read it back you. Can tell the Judges in terms of the discussions of Herceg-Bosna in this transcript that we've just read, how that fits into your conclusions that Herceg-Bosna continued to exist and operate after Washington and Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness answer that question could it be just be made clear for the record whether these presidential transcripts were documents that the witness considered in writing his paper whether they were provided to him by the Prosecution, and whether he found them on his own research? And I refer to all the transcripts, not just this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miller, this document, this presidential document, did you have this document before or are you just discover it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have it in preparing my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have also a question. Pages 40 to 58 are blank. There's a number for the page, but they're blank. Is there an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is. The reasons for that is that in order to keep -- because of the translations of the excerpts that have been made and the entire -- first of all, let me back up. The entire B/C/S original transcript has been provided to the Defence some time ago. In preparing translations, some of the translations were only done of certain excerpted material, thinking that it was not wise to burden the translation resources of this institution with 30 or 40 pages of irrelevant material. In order to keep the pagination exactly the same between the English version and the original B/C/S, the page numbers were -- were inserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness might be allowed to answer question that's now been put to him twice, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that in these passages we see a concern, especially -- I would point to the concern over the -- of the standard of living of the Croatian population, and I -- I read this to mean that the -- that the government of Herceg-Bosna is concerned to maintain a higher standard of living for the Croats of the region. When Mr. Prlic says, "Every Croat in Bosnia-Herzegovina is a paid Croat," that obviously refers to the fact that they're all employed. They're all doing well. And I think that -- it seems to me it's clear that what they're trying to do is make sure that there is no cause for the Croats of the region to look any place else for sustenance, political or otherwise. I would leave it at that, but I think it shows clear signs that they're focused on the Croatian population, and disinterested at best in the overall Bosnian question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to then go to the final exhibit in the Prosecution's examination, that is P 08545, which is an another presidential transcript. P 08545. Apparently in the second binder. Thank you, Your Honour. If you have that, Dr. Miller. And this is a transcript from again a meeting on the 27th of March of 1995. And if I could once again please direct your attention to the bottom of page 14 and just indicate that is Mr. Prlic talking at this point. And then continuing over to page 15, second sentence -- well, the first full sentence beginning on that page: "At this moment those three areas of the federation function as two state entities and as two completely separate states within its internal structure. They are the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, these are territories controlled by the republic of BH army. Why do I say two states? According to all the constituent elements, these are two completely different states." And he refers and talks about, for example, the customs procedures. Going to the next paragraph at the bottom of that same page Mr. Prlic continues and says: "Mr. President, as far as the federation is concerned, nothing has been done so far in the functional sense. Not a single function of the federation has been developed. Therefore, these are all just a few psychological effects. It exists or it does not exist. However, not a single function of the federation has been established ..." And then continuing over on to page 16. Below the middle of the page and Mr. Prlic is continuing to speak: "Mr. President, today we as the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are working in five to eight separate areas. You can imagine the difficulties in travelling from one area to another, in the movement of goods, securing customs, taxes and everything else. However, a system is in place. We have completed the transformation of the HVO, the police, and health care. We have attained a certain level in the standard of living which Jozo was correct -- corrected after this increase. An elementary schoolteacher will have about 1.100 kuna," which is Croatian currency. "Mr. President, people are being born and dying and die with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, it is both their birth and death certificate and the flag under which they are buried. That has infiltrated all the people's pours down there, and therefore people are both emotionally and profoundly connected to this." And if I could then go on to the next page, please. Below the half of the page -- on the bottom half of the page 17, and I'll leave it at this and won't go on to any other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRLIC CONTINUES
utterances.text: "Relations with the Republic of Croatia. They are the way they are. They are partially maintained outside the law through private channels, et cetera. I understand that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna is neither an internationally recognised subject nor can it operate publicly nor can a document be adopted to regulate it. Here I would like to emphasise the exceptionally correct relations with the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Health, and Ministry of the Interior. Therefore, these are exemplary relations with the real integral Croatian identity, at least in my view if I may say so, has reached full expression. Mr. President, often today Herceg-Bosna is used for daily political needs. I do not whose here. I analyse the political scene." And my similar question to you, Dr. Miller, is how do those passages fit into your conclusions that Herceg-Bosna continued to exist and function after the Washington and Dayton peace agreements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard not to conclude from these as passages that the government of Herceg-Bosna was more concerned with its relations with Croatia, with maintaining its government functions, securing customs, taxes, movement of goods, everything else I'm quoting. There's absolutely no reference whatsoever to any of these functions fading away. And then of course emphasising things that "people are being born and dying and die within the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as both their birth and death and the flag under which they are buried that has infiltrated all the people's pours down there" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Okay. "Infiltrated all the people's pours down there." This is just a you know, a fairly fluid way of saying that there is very little intention of seeing Herceg-Bosna dissolved into something that's not totally Croatian. I'm sorry for my fast reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Miller that concludes my examination on behalf of the Prosecution, and I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and providing your testimony. Mr. President, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is actually time to take a break now, so we will take a break of 20 minutes and resume right after the break and the cross-examinations will begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours. 12

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and I'll begin by asking you some general questions. More or less we'll start with your second report, the persistence of Herceg-Bosna after the Washington Agreement and Dayton. Sir, in preparation for this report, how much time did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I originally had about -- I suppose a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was back when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the spring of 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it would be fair to say that you've had plenty of time from 2006 up until today to revise this report if you had decided or if the Prosecutor decided that you should revise it; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I've noticed that in the first report you indicate that a question was posed to you. With respect to the second one I don't see you starting off with a question, you know, sort of a mission statement. So my question is: What exactly did the Prosecutor ask you to do concretely? And by that I mean, did they submit to you some sort of a letter, memorandum, or was it just over the phone, a conversation, and then you took it from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In both -- in both cases they submitted a topic for me to analyse. Although the question doesn't appear in the second report, there was a question just as there was in the first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say a topic, was that orally or written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you have that with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it a one-sheet page or is it more than one or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a one-sheet page that had both --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Both topics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- both reports were there, and they were very short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it would have been up to you, you being the qualified expert, historian, to decide what if any material, resources would you need for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did they provide you with a list of documents that you might wish to consult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they provide you with any documents, physical -- you know, electronically or what have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we talking about second report or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Second report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ask for any documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You seem like puzzled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not puzzled about the question I'm just trying to remember if I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did you provide more -- did you provide a draft or was this the final version, here it is, take it or leave it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not the final version but very little was done to it in between first draft and this draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So this is the second and final draft or might there be a third and a fourth draft. And I'm not talking about commas and, you know, paragraphs. I'm talking about substantive changes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. There actually were never substantive changes to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So although I suppose technically some things were done to it that rise to the level above commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at any point in time did the Prosecution ask you to perhaps look at any particular material after they saw your first draft, or were they just happy? And that could be the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I think they did give me one document. It was the speech by Ante Markovic, but I don't believe it made it into the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, since writing the report and before coming here to testify, did you review any other documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since writing the report before coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arriving on the plane? No I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when you did arrive in The Hague, that's when they showed you these newly disclosed newly discovered documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that included some of the presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you -- were you aware-- let me rephrase. You -- you do know that there are a large volume of presidential transcripts, that President Tudjman would tape record some of his meetings and that they exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've known about that for some time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you've read them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the entire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Collection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Run, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever ask for the Prosecution to provide them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the ones that were shown to you today in court, I take it they showed you those transcripts when you were being proofed, prepared to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did they show you the entire batch and say, here, look at it, see what you can glean from it, pull out some passages, you know, feed me the question that I might want to ask you, or did they say I'm going to ask you about this passage here, that passage there, and then you go ahead and provide whatever interpretation you wish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the two -- I saw the two full meeting records that those passages were drawn from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in my version, because I only read English, a lot of pages are missing, and it was pointed out by Judge Trechsel that we have segments that are just blank pages, but they're numbered in any event. Did you by any chance read those transcripts in their entirety since you read Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware. I did not read them in their entirety. I skimmed sort of the Croatian versions in their entirety, and I read significant portions of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it in preparation of your report, the second report that you wrote, you would have looked at the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you're not -- is that -- is that like a definitive yes or is that like probably yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking if I looked at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you looked at it, if you studied it, if you reviewed it in preparation for this particular report, because we're talking about Washington and Dayton. So did you look at the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it, you being an historian, you would have been aware of or you researched everything that preceded Washington, the Washington Agreement, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything? I mean, there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A historian and everything, there's an enormous sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll play it by a different way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm not trying to play games.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you follow the events that led up to the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And there were lots of negotiations, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the reason I point that out is that we're going to get to this one section. In your very first footnote you quote Roger Cohen and you say that -- and first you get Mr. Prlic's title wrong. If Cohen got it wrong, shame on you for getting it wrong because you should know better, but in any event it says here, the quote: "No interest in a unitary government in Bosnia and are only interested in federal institutions in confederation of Croatia." That's in footnote 1 of your second report. Now, that worth unitary -- let me first finish which is -- you then go on to say: "This attitude expressed with this sort of clarity would not diminish until nearly a decade later." Sir, did you ever bother to read the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read the Dayton Peace Accords, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And annexed to the Dayton Peace Accords you would find what, among other things? Would you not find the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that a yes or okay if you're telling me, I'll buy it? Which of the two? This is not a kidding matter. I need to know. Did you read the entire Dayton Peace Accords, because there are lots of annexes to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read the entire Dayton Peace Accords. I did not read them immediately before writing this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever bother to read the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina that's annexed to the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read the entire document with its annexes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when was that? Was that back in 1995 when things were unfolding, slightly thereafter? Did you read it in preparation for this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not read it in preparation for this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you read by any chance the other two constitutions that are annexed to the Dayton Peace Accords? And you might -- do you know what other constitutions I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read the Dayton Peace Accords about nine years ago and since then I've referred to them but no I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you did not read the other two constitutions that were annexed to the Dayton Peace Accords. And I'm talking about the constitution of the Federation and the constitution of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's take a step back into memory lane. Before the Dayton Peace Accord we have the Washington Agreement. What was the Washington Agreement about, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Washington agreement was about making peace between the Croats and the Muslims. It was the brainchild of the US government. I believe that the -- you know, in the big picture, the US wanted Croatia and the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina to begin to get along better so that they could concentrate on the so-called Serbian aspect of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was it just a one sheet of paper agreement or were there aspects to the Washington Agreement that called into place various relationships, let's say? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's sort of a vague question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, part of the Washington Agreement was there -- was there any special relationship between, say, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was understood that Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina would have the -- or excuse me, that the Muslim-Croat portion would have a confederal relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say it was understood, understood what, in the philosophical sense or was it in part of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't recall. All right. Do you recall any details in the Washington Agreement related to details between Herceg-Bosna, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna at that point in time, and, say, the federation, and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the creation of the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I recall any details?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm asking you this because you're writing a paper about the Washington Agreement, and the reason I'm asking you these questions and I hope the Trial Chamber is picking up on this, and I'm sure they are, is because the Washington Agreement had all sorts of matters to it that needed to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one would think that if you are commenting about the Washington Agreement you would know what it is that the two parties had to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Not wanting to interrupt, but I don't think that states the proper nature of the witness's testimony, the report that he prepared. He was not asked to study or give a report on the Washington Agreement. The question was a very specific and narrow one. Did Herceg-Bosna continue to exist and function after the Washington Agreement, and I submit to the -- to Your Honours respectfully that to answer that question you only needed to know one thing about the Washington Agreement and that is the date. Did Herceg-Bosna continue to exist after Washington was signed at the end of February 1994, and you can answer that question without knowing word one about the Washington Agreement, and it's a mischaracterisation by Mr. Karnavas to say that this man was asked to write a report or give any views about the Washington Agreement. That is not correct and it's not fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If I may respond very briefly, Your Honours. And if I had misquoted the gentleman's submission, then I apologise. Obviously he wasn't supposed to write about the Washington Agreement per se. However, one would say time that if he's going to write about the persistence of Herceg-Bosna, one would have to know what is in the Washington Agreement, because -- you're shaking are head Judge Trechsel. Let me finish before you conclude and before you jump to conclusions. You're pre-judging the case. I suggest that if you look at the Washington Agreement it is not like coming into court and switching on that light. Things like that may happen in other parts of Western Europe, but we're talking about a country in transition. We're talking about a place where the space of Bosnia-Herzegovina, most of it have was under occupation and there was a war going on, and I dare say if you read the Washington Agreement and if you look at what was -- what needed to be implemented in the Washington Agreement, it called for the continuation of Herceg-Bosna until the transitional period ended. And that what I want to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, that is a legal argument. You're talking as a lawyer. The expert here is as a historian and not as a lawyer. He is not -- he was not asked to say whether it was okay if Herceg-Bosna continued to exist. That was not the question. You're telling us it was supposed to continue. That's okay but that's an evaluation which the witness was obviously not asked to give and did not give I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What -- well, if you look at -- if you wish to look at this trial in a vacuum, and you may choose to do so, Judge Trechsel, you may choose to do so, if you wish to look at it in a vacuum we can go on with what the Prosecutor is saying, look at a date and move on. If on the other hand you have to look at the facts and circumstances as they were unfolding in an agreement that calls for a transitional period. One would think if you're talking about persistence, and you're call -- calling this person to come in as an historian, you would have to see whether those who were involved in Herceg-Bosna were complying with the implementation of the Washington Agreement given what was available at the time and given what was happening on the ground. The same thing with Dayton. If you are to look at what is happening today in Bosnia, it is still in the transitional phase. So to say that all of a sudden, you know, as of this date are they persisting. Well, the documents say that they have to persist. The laws that were placed in Herceg-Bosna were to continue if they were not in contradiction with the constitution until such time as they were replaced. Now, if the gentleman is going to come in here and opine and to say that the Croats were continuing in some sort of policy, one would think that he would have come here prepared. But obviously Judge Trechsel you seem to be indifferent to this sort of information and that's why I said initially, if we're going to go down this route, we're going to be talking about the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accords. We're going to be talking about post conflict reconstruction in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You've opened up the Pandora's box, I did not. And that's why I have to go in -- and what I'm trying to demonstrate is the gentleman hasn't looked at these vital documents. So to simply look at a date and say are they still persisting in a vacuum is unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I suggest Mr. Karnavas might want to take a breath. I think it's -- my first objection is to -- the way that he has engaged with Judge Trechsel. I don't think it's appropriate. I don't think counsel needs to raise his voice and to show that kind of emotion and respond to a completely appropriate comment by Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The shaking of the head by Judge Trechsel in the middle of my argument I take it as a prejudgement of the facts, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Calm down, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't need a lecture from you sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Calm down. Secondly, Your Honour, I join and Judge Trechsel in that regard, did state the point quite correctly, and I join in that to clarify my earlier comments. And if Mr. Karnavas wants to have an argument about the scope of the report, he can have that with me. The witness did what the witness was asked to do, and it was a very narrow question. And as Judge Trechsel properly said, it wasn't -- it was at no time a question of was it justified to continue, was it proper to continue, under what basis? The witness was simply asked to confirm, did it continue to exist and operate after Dayton and Washington and the answer -- the witness's answer is yes. And he was not -- and I want to make it very clear to the Chamber in fairness to witness, the witness was not asked to research either Washington or Dayton and it was not pertinent to the specific question he was asked to address. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on I'll move on very well very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will continue. But actually you were in agreement with Mr. Karnavas. He wanted to know whether you had read the Washington Accords and you answered yes, you have read them, I have read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the Dayton Peace Accords were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the Dayton Peace Accords we find the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does it call for unitary government, yes, no or I don't recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you mean you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that's the correct answer because there's a difference between I don't recall and I don't know. I don't know means I'm ignorant, I don't know that. I don't recall means I forgot. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall. At this moment I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the reason I'm asking is because you're talking about -- you're quoting Roger Cohen and saying this attitude expressed in the context of the unitary government that Mr. Prlic is quoted. What does he mean by unitary government if you know? What is a unitary government in the context in which Dr. Prlic indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want you to assume. I want you to tell me whether you know or not. If you don't know we'll move on. Because if you don't know that basic fundamental issue then everything else that flows is false. So do you know in what context he's saying unitary government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would respectfully suggest that having never spoken with Mr. Prlic I can only assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me how the term then was used back then during the discussions, and this was an ongoing discussion 1991, 1992, 1993, 2007. So you tell me, Mr. Historian, what is meant here by unitary government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A unitary government would be a centralised government, a single government governing all of the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina presumably without any sort of federal arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was -- what was the whole issue leading up to the Washington Agreement and leading up to Dayton with all the parties with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Wasn't it against having a unitary government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally the sides were opposed to a unitary government, the Croats and Serbs especially for the most part. There were those who favoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There were those who favoured it. You said that you looked at all of the peace agreements. As back as 1992 were there not peace agreements on the table that called for three -- there were various proposals, but in essence that all three constituent peoples would be protected within the state but that they would have either their own republics, or they would have certain areas which they would manage depending on the minority status of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when Washington -- when the Dayton Peace Accords were negotiated, did -- did the constitution that was ultimately drafted, was that for unitary government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was for a strong federation and a strong Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell me -- you talk about in page 2, you say social and other services are handled by Herceg-Bosna rather than through BiH government. And then there's footnote number 4. I want to ask you, sir, in 1994 what sort of services did the BiH government provide to its citizens, and I'm talking outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was it not a fact, sir, assuming you do know what was happening at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it not a fact that at the local level folks were organising themselves and trying to do the best they could, whether it was having a monitoring system or introducing their own monitoring system or using foreign currencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the Washington Agreement comes into play, how much of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina is -- is free, liberated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When which agreement comes into play?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How much of Bosnia was free?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.
