utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That actually would depend upon the perspective from which we're talking. I mean, the Serbs felt they had a free zone. The Croats felt they had one. If you're asking me about the Muslim portion of Bosnia, not much, but I couldn't put a percentage on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When the Muslims and the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed a federation, how much of that territory are we talking about? And I'm talking pre-Dayton, post Washington.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How much of it was free?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. How much was it Bosnia-Herzegovina to speak of that was non-occupied by the Republika Srpska forces, the VRS, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Because you're talking about the persistence of Herceg-Bosna, and I'm wondering if the local government cannot provide any social services as you just admitted, and if at the local level somebody has got to pay for salaries, pensions and so on and so forth. Why is it that it is any surprise that Herceg-Bosna has to continue in providing those services?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I just want to note again in light of the comments and questions that have already been raised a continuing objection to these questions. I take it from the continuing direction of the questions that in fact there is no dispute that Herceg-Bosna continued to exist and function after both Washington and Dayton and Mr. Karnavas does not agree -- does not disagree with that and his only argument is that its continued existence and function was justified. But since he only --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Since the only reason that the witness was brought to give his second report was to confirm the continued existence and operation of Herceg-Bosna, that is not in dispute. His report is accepted as true in that respect, and Mr. Karnavas only wants to argue whether it was justified to continue operating existing or not which is a separate question which as Judge Trechsel has said, as I've said, is beyond the scope of what this witness was asked to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let my address the Prosecutor on this and let me disabuse him of any notion. I don't know what Judge Trechsel knows or doesn't know about the Washington Agreement, the Dayton Peace Accords, what's happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We do have legal documents. Some documents have come in thus far, and those documents show exactly what the responsibilities are during this transitional period. I'm going from a legal basis, what the documents call for. I'm not going to show them to the gentleman because, one, I don't have time because I don't -- we physically cannot do that; and two, he's not a lawyer. But what I'm trying to show, the point that I'm trying to make, is how deceptively dishonest of the Prosecution is, the office the Prosecution, is trying to say as of this date if Herceg-Bosna continued it must have been -- it must -- all activities were illegal because they had this joint criminal enterprise. And what I'm trying to show is this gentleman at least had two years to prepare a report and could have had and he is an historian and had access to all these documents, would have been able to say at least one, what did this transitional period call for? Two, what was happening during this transitional period? Three, what were the sides doing? Because if we look at the reports that are coming from the International Crisis Group, and of course the gentleman cherry picked, but if you look at them and you look at them completely, you will see that trying to implement the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Peace Accords is a can of worms. It is terribly difficult and complex, and you cannot look at just one thing. For instance, and I'll move on to the military, what were the arrangements as a result of the Washington Accords and even the Dayton Accords? What were the arrangements as far as the defence, the different militaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I was a bit thinking if I have to take the floor and to mention to you that I really do not agree with your characterisation of the Prosecution as dishonest. I really feel that it is not very good to characterise each other here in this courtroom as dishonest or whatever. You may say that you do not agree with it, you may say that it is not well based, well founded, et cetera, but I think that if we start calling each other's position and view as dishonest, then we cannot go further and we cannot achieve our, in a way, major aim, which is of course to find the just position in between the parties. So I would of course like to say the same thing to everyone, and to the Prosecution as well, and to everyone here in the courtroom, but I really believe that this kind of invectives are not correct to be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take your point, but it is intellectually dishonest, in my opinion, and disingenuous to be saying all you need to do is look at one date in a vacuum without look at what were the implementing documents calling for. That's what I'm suggesting. And if you're going to buy this report without any of that, then it seems to me we're wasting our time. You look at the Dayton Peace Accords, you look at what it calls for what the parties are to do only looking at that can you write a report saying whether Herceg-Bosna was -- continued to exist illegally, because there were certain functions that kept going on by virtue of the agreement and arrangement of the parties. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Karnavas, do you take the illegally in the context of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I read the report, Your Honour. I read the report. And I don't know what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing the word "illegally" in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe it's an oversight. I'm not perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "These illegal structures operated." It's on paragraph 2, Your Honour, middle of the page. It says "In the aftermath of the Washington Agreement, the government of Herceg-Bosna continued to function as it had before the agreement." It's on the second report, Your Honour, page 1, paragraph 2. It did so via institutions it had established before the signing of the Washington Agreement with the assistance (financial and moral) of the government of Croatia. These illegal --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It wreaks with illegality. And what I'm saying and I don't mean to be disrespectful, but having been in Bosnia and worked on this transitional period, it is not like switching on the light switch over there. There is a whole series of processes, and we're going to go through this entire Dayton Peace Accords at some point in light of the testimony that's coming in today and that's what I was trying to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's get back to the constitution of BiH. What services, sir, did the state retain by virtue of the constitution? Which one did it retain and which one it gave to the two entities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to interrupt you, Mr. Karnavas, but following to what you've requested from the witness on the Washington Accords. Witness, looking at both of your reports I have the feeling that there are two elements which you don't mention and which I find in minutes of the Presidency. It seems that Mr. Kissinger wrote an article in the Washington Post. Did you read this article written by Mr. Kissinger? And also the former American Ambassador, Zimmermann, wrote a book entitled the origins of the catastrophe. Did you also see this book? Did you also consult it or read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read the work by Warren Zimmermann as a matter of course. It's my field and so I read it. But I did not read it in preparing this report. Respectfully I don't know which article by Mr. Kissinger you're referring, but I've certainly read articles by Henry Kissinger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, for instance, what about defence? How was defence handled in the constitution of BiH as a result of Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean to the specificity that you undoubtedly are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay. I'm trying to be calm here. What about -- let's just say finance, budget, taxes, administration, customs, collection? Was that handled at the state or was that handled -- given to the entities to do, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about education, science, and culture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it seems to me that you're making certain assertions in your report without really knowing what was provided for the entities and what the state was supposed to do, and I -- and the reason -- I'm not trying to pick on you, but you say in here "Social services and other services are handled by Herceg-Bosna rather than through BiH government, BiH government." This is page 2. It's the top of -- and then you have a footnote, and you are citing some report. And one would think that if you're going to make such a bold statement, you would know what sort of social services, for instance, the government of BiH has because of the constitution which Herceg-Bosna supposedly is running and refusing to cooperate with the government as it would appear, my interpretation of what you're saying here. Would it surprise you, sir, that the -- that the constitution of BiH calls for the following: Foreign policy, foreign trade, they have a customs policy, monetary policy, finances, immigration, international and interentity criminal law enforcement, establishment and operation of common and international communication facilities, regulations of the inner entity transportation, air traffic? But if we go to the constitutions for the entities now, we see at the very top, and this is -- it's under Article 5 -- at some point we'll introduce these documents, but at the very top it says "Defence." Is it not a fact, sir, that as a result of both -- of the Dayton Peace Accords you had two armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina because that's what what was agreed, one for the federation and one for the VRS? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact it took many, many years and a lot of cajoling and arm twisting by the internationals in order to merge those armies even though the constitution calls for the defence to be under the entities? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you agree with me being an historian that thus far the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina has not been amended, otherwise you would have had to amend the Dayton Peace Accords because it's annexed to it. Do you know whether it was amended or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you look to see whether it had been amended? I mean, don't you think that if you're going to be talking about what sort of services that Herceg-Bosna has retained and refuses to cooperate that you would at least look and see whether it was within their domain in light of the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't concerned with what was in their domain. I was concerned with the situation as it stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would it -- would you agree with me that it would be helpful to at least know about it? We don't need any comments from Mr. Scott otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can object, you can object, but you don't have to give the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, what do you object to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I note the concerning objection, Your Honour and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, but let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've made the objection, I've made the objection, and I think the Court needs to give some further direction on the proper scope and direction of cross-examination on this point. I repeat what I said earlier. It appears to me, and I'm just saying it appears to me, and the Judges will each have to make your own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm making my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've already made your objection. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now he's made his objection it's a standing objection. A standing objection means it's continuing. It doesn't mean that he gets to stand up every too often -- so often to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's inappropriate to continue to suggest to this witness wouldn't you have wanted to consider this, don't you think you should have considered this and whether it was justified or not whether when that was not the question that the witness was asked to address and it's just inappropriate. It's just simply in -- let's just talk about anything we want to. Let's have no rules whatsoever. Let's have a free for all. The only question the witness was asked to address is did Herceg-Bosna continue to exist and operate after this time? Again what I hear Mr. Karnavas saying is that he agrees that it did but that it was justified. Now that's a separate point and he can call other -- he can say that as much as he wants and he can justify it, but only point was with this witness to respond to a number of things that have been said and suggested that Herceg-Bosna was a temporary organisation. It never meant to be a state. It never did these things, and it now it appears that it's clear that's not the case. And so Mr. Karnavas has changed the issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- no longer wants to argue about the continued existence of Herceg-Bosna. Now he simply wants to argue that it was justified. That's a different argument and one that this witness was not asked to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now if Mr. -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If Mr. Scott would like to say it one more time so he doesn't have to interrupt me again. I heard it the first time. There was no need to get up and say it all over again for the second time. You know. Well, Judge Trechsel he's right. I need some guidance from the Court. Either tell me to stop and move on in which case you rule on the objection, you sustain it, or you find that what I'm doing is relevant and I continue. I'm going by his report. His report here talks about, for instance, on page 2, it says here at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is relevant is what I understand. Mr. Karnavas, you want to show by your questions that the Washington Accords have in some way given an existence to Herceg-Bosna. Is that -- is that what you are trying to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to show, Your Honour, is that in if we're going to introduce this sort of document in, and if you're going to have this sort of expert come in to talk about a subject that is very, very complicated, that one would expect the expert to be prepared for this discussion, and that's what I'm trying to show, that this gentleman here is not qualified. I indicated so when I filed my objection, that he's not qualified to talk about these events. First of all, they're beyond the indictment and second of all and more importantly he needs to have the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague, Judge Trechsel, told you that the expert witness is not a lawyer, is not a jurist. He is a historian. But as a rule, perhaps I'm not in agreement with my colleague, but a historian should have some legal knowledge. In particular, he should know the scope of the constitution or an international agreement to gather some historical conclusions, findings. Therefore, you ask him if the constitution had been amended. He answered I don't know. So continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will. I will. I don't mean to be obstreperous. It's just I look and see what the gentleman has is cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's look at the bottom of page 2 you say that Miroslav -- I can't pronounce his name Miroslav Prce I think it is. The defence minister of the federation of Bosna-Herzegovina argued as late as August 1999 that "The Croat side does not support a unified army in BiH because we do not want to create another mini former JNA." Now, you recall you were asked a question by the Prosecutor regarding this. Now, you say -- over here you quote -- somebody is quoted. Unified army in BiH. So we're not talking about an army that's unified within the federation. We're talking about an army that's unified within BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in 1999, do you know whether the RS had its own army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Getting back to the Washington and then post-Dayton. How many international organisations were involved in the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accords, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By number, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the relevance, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the Dayton Peace Accords call for a central bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did a central bank exist prior to the Dayton Peace Accords that was functioning in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about when -- when the federation is formed, was it formed before or after the Dayton peace accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim-Croat federation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, is there another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during that period of time please discuss -- describe to us the transitional process in order to harmonise the laws, the payment schemes, the pension plans, the salaries and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there -- did that agreement call for some sort of an implementation programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were the salaries -- were the salaries in BiH uniform as a result of -- immediately after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's forget about the RS. What about within the federation. Were there not cantons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many cantons were in the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what were the functions or the responsibilities of the cantons vis-a-vis the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I could specify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were all cantons on the same payment scheme as far as salaries, pensions, and what have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know, how do you know whether one of side or the other is -- is acting inappropriately or illegally as you put it in here, these illegal institutions, whatever institutions you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you -- let me read the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's -- I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You don't need to. I just need to read it. I suppose in terms of salaries and pensions I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, who was responsible for salaries and pensions? Was it the state? Was it at the local level? Was it somewhere in between at say the entity level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Who is responsible for the universities? Was that at the state level or at the entity level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the -- the soldiers and the invalids in particular? Who paid for them? You know, post-Dayton. How was that arranged? Was that at the state level, the entity level, or sort of at the nationalistic level in the is sense that if you belong the ABiH, the HVO or the VRS? Do you know anything about that? Who was responsible to take care of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Constitutionally, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about utility services? Was that at the state level or was that at the -- at the entity level or was it further down at the cantonal level? Which of the three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To what extent was Herceg-Bosna cooperating, say for instance, in trying to make its payments to -- to say salaries, pensions and what have you? Do you know whether they were making those payments? I mean, we read something in the document here. Let's take Mostar, for instance. Who was paying for the salaries of the teachers in Mostar, say the west side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, who was responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. This is all according to Dayton; right? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, according to Dayton or even the Washington Agreement. What about the army? Who was supposed to pay the salaries of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now this quote, getting back to the quote on page 2 when you talk about that the Croats did not support a unified army in BiH, and you're quoting somebody. If the constitutions call for two separate defences, one for the federation and one for the RS, assuming that you knew that, how then can you adopt this particular statement as being true, accurate and complete? And if you don't understand the question I'll can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you don't need to. It's a quote. It's a quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've adopted the quote. You've adopted --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I attributed it to a fellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you put it in there as if this is part of your conclusion. You're reading somebody, you're quoting. This gives it authority. So now you have some sort of authority to make this bold statement. This is part of the conclusion of which you want this Trial Chamber to adopt. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to my previous questions, if you hadn't read the constitutions, if you did not know that under Dayton you had two defences and the entities were responsible for the defence, that was the madness of Dayton, you had two militaries pointing inward, okay, how can you then, say, adopt this quote as being accurate simply because it comes out of some -- some other report where it says, the Croat side does not support a unified army in BiH when the constitution itself does not call for a uniform army in BiH in 1999? How on earth can you do that with a straight face under oath in front of these Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It sounds like we both agree that the comment is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the contrary, sir. The comment cannot being accurate in a sense because you're saying that the Croat side does not support a unified army. What I'm saying is the constitution, the greatest law of the land, one that the parties negotiated, called for two separate army, one for the federation, one for the RS. So the constitution doesn't provide. So how can you then say here, blame the Croats for supposedly not wanting a unified -- a unified army when in fact the contusion doesn't call for one and neither did the parties negotiate for that at Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't blame the Croats. I quoted a gentleman stating what apparently is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I did it under oath because I am not lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know at the time, did you know, sir, I want a straight answer here, did you know at the time when you took this quote and you put it into your report, did you know at the time that under Dayton, under the constitution of BiH, under the constitution of the Republika Srpska, under the constitution of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it called for the defences to be under the entities and not, I repeat not under the state; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know Dayton verbatim, but I did know they were supposed to be separate armies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well why didn't you put that in your report? Why did you just take this quote and put it in your there? What was the purpose of it? If you knew already that constitution of the Croats didn't have to have a unified army because you would have had to have the Serbs and the Muslims and Bosniaks at this point all agree to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It served to contribute to my answer to the question I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see. Exactly. It severed to contribute where you wanted to go with this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm saying it. All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miller, with regard to this issue of the unified army, while Mr. Karnavas was asking you these questions, I was looking at page 2, what you wrote, and I think that in fact what you write, well, it's a declaration of the defence minister of the federation, Mr. Miroslav Prce who is supposed to have said that. And you quote this declaration, footnote 7, drawn from the report of the 28th of October, 1999. So it -- I get the feeling that it's not your conclusion. You are referring to what was said by the defence minister of the federation, and you have of incorporated it into your report. Now, did you agree with this vision, with this concept, or this way of seeing things? If you quote him, it would suggest that you agree, or do you quote him as an historian might do saying, Well, someone said such-and-such. This is to inform the reader. Do you understand what I'm trying to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand what you're trying to say, but I'm not sure I understand the distinction in this case. I mean, it was a statement drawn in support of an argument that the Croats of Herceg-Bosna are reluctant to see their state structures disappear. I don't really view this as something -- it's not a vision or a concept that I agree with or disagree with. It's a piece of evidence in an argument that Herceg-Bosna is not going away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. With the authorisation of Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. President, since this examination is becoming problematic for the whole process, I think that it is important to focus on the previous part of the sentence. What we're dealing with here in all the questions posed by my Defence lawyer is some -- based on the evidence that is going to be introduced. Before that quotation by the defence minister, there's the observation by the historian which says that the desire for separation extended to virtually all manifestation of statehood. And that quotation just served us to -- him to confirm the standpoint already put forward by him. My Defence lawyer is showing clearly that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a state that did not have one army. So it's not a question of statehood. And it is not the object of an expert witness to prove the actions of Herceg-Bosna, and that is why we wanted to challenge every sentence quoted by him, because he clearly indicates the -- his standpoint. Every sentence in his expert report is a problematic one, and that is why we're challenging it through the questions. For example, the first sentence: [In English] "There is little evidence that the Croatian side had any intention of giving up its authority in Herceg-Bosna." [Interpretation] Now, Defence counsel is authorised to challenge this position, and that is what he did. The second sentence: "[In English] Nor did the leadership of the so proclaimed Republic of Herceg-Bosna try to hide its intent to maintain the autonomy of the region and even see it attached to Croatia." [Interpretation] My Defence counsel is quite right in challenging that position, because this exhibit is part of the proceedings. The third sentence -- the expert doesn't know my post, my function, but he has a clear stand when he speaks about the building of the a federation and confederation. He says this attitude expressed with this sort of clarity would not diminish until nearly a decade later. Now, if the position put forward by me is absolutely in conformity with the constitution, then my defence does have the right to challenge this position. The following sentence: "[In English] The government of Herceg-Bosna continued to function as it had before the agreement." [Interpretation] We have the right to challenge the objectivity of that position both through the constitution of the federation and the functions that Herceg-Bosna had and the part that was under BH army control. Now, the next sentence "These illegal structures." [Interpretation] So we have the right to challenge expert says here. On the following page: "[In English] Social and other services rather via Herzeg-Bosna rather than through the BH government." [Interpretation] Once again we have the right to use the constitution because the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not provide for a single social function to take place at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina without going any further. And that is why I would like the cross-examination to continue because we wish to challenge each of these statements and that is our absolute right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, would you like to respond to the comments made by Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just in general. I just have to -- in light of what's been going on, I think it's only fair for the Prosecution to have a couple of minutes in given all the time that both the Defence and some of the accused have taken. This is what the Chamber has witnessed this afternoon is a complete shift from a position that Herceg-Bosna did not continue to exist, did not continue to function well after both Dayton and Washington, and in the face of this witness's evidence and other evidence in the case, that can no longer possibly be denied. And what we've now shifted is to an attempt to justify its continued existence which is an entirely different position again and not the one that this witness was asked to address and we now -- it's a moving target. It's a moving target, and now we're talking about something entirely different. And I have to suggest, Your Honour, it's entirely unfair to this witness. The witness is brought to address the question A, and then he is criticised for not addressing question R. He was never asked to address question R. He was asked to address question A. And I think it's -- to put the continued questions to the witness for no other real purpose except to embarrass the witness about details of the Dayton agreement that I don't think any of us would necessarily remember off the top of our heads without having the document in front of us, is unfair and irrelevant to what the question -- to what the witness was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when the Defence asks him questions relating to the B question, the witness says, well, I don't know. So in fact he's only answering in regard to question A about which he is an expert. So it's quite clear. Mr. Karnavas, you may pursue. Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say that I was misunderstood. I'm not speaking about whether Herceg-Bosna existed or not or whether it should have existed or not. All we're talking about here is that this report should not be accepted and adopted. I'm just talking about this expert report, that it cannot be found acceptable. And the sense of the questions we're asking is to challenge it as an expert report. Now, whether you're going to conclude whether it did exist or not that's your right, but through our questions we wish to say that this expert report is unacceptable, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever bother to look at the transitional arrangements that are actually in the -- in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And that would be under Article 11. Did you look at those transitional arrangements? Because now since you're talking about a period of post-Dayton, that would be post 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, you know, as I'm sure you can imagine there's some sort of a transitional arrangement, and we see that in Iraq, something that the bush Administration failed to see. They thought they would just take over Baghdad and that would be the end of it and we see that there is a huge transitional period. So did you look at the transitional arrangements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, under Article 11, it tells us to look at Article -- at annex 2, and annex 2 of the BiH constitution says that 1, joint interim commission. The parties hereby establish a joint interim commission with a mandate to discuss practical questions related to the implementation of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the general framework agreement and its annexes and to make recommendations and proposals. Now, in your preparation for this report, did you look to see what was happening with this joint interim commission and to see what, if anything, the Croats were doing within that commission in furtherance of the implementation process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It then goes on to B, just to make sure we know who are in this commission, the joint interim commission shall be composed of four persons from the federation, three persons from the Republika Srpska, and one representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then it goes on under 2 constitution -- I'm sorry, continuation of laws. Continuation of laws. "All laws, regulations, and judicial rules of procedure in effect within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina when the constitution enters into force shall remain in effect to the extent not inconsistent with the constitution until otherwise determined by a competent government body of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Were you aware of that transitional arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does it make sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I assume -- or we could assume that just as the Croats had organised themselves, the Muslims, you know, the Bosniaks, had organised themselves as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you had the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but for all intents and purposes during the war you had a siege in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had places like in Tuzla where they were self-managing to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you bother to look and see whether there was parity in the services that were being provided in those communities and in those areas vis-a-vis the services and salaries and what have you that were being provided in areas that were under or part of the initially the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, later on the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Did you look into that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any transitional provisions for the harmonisation of that process and what that process called for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, you didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you -- I take it you would also assume that that's what the international community has been doing since 1995 in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the international community's been involved, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That it had been involved, for instance, in trying to establish one, I think they call it, economic space; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you saying okay because you don't know or -- I don't want you to accept my -- you know, what I'm claiming to be fact, but do you know that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I accept what you say as fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know up until what time you had different systems with respect to customs? And I'm talking about the RS, the federation, cantonal level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any transitional arrangements for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I assume it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Who pays for the state government? Where does it get its income from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just in the time that we have left for the -- for the rest of the time, if you could just help me out here and just please describe what exactly you did in trying to come up with this report, assuming that you wanted to have a report that was fair, balanced, and informative, keeping in mind that you are a Ph.D. from a very fine university where you're taught how to do research. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did what I was asked to do, which was provide a short, directed report on the nature or persistence or non-persistence, I suppose, of the government of Herceg-Bosna, and I did so as I was asked on the basis of open-source materials, knowing that I was not going to be able to afford to or be supported in going and doing on-site research and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You're piquing my interest now here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The constitution it can be found on -- I have a hard copy from my days in OHR but it can be found on the internet can it not? I mean, just the way you found all these documents from the international crisis group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Dayton Accords can be found on the internet, and like I've told you I have read and understood the Dayton Accords in the past. I do not know them in detail, and I did not go back to study them in the detail because I did not feel - and I do have a Ph.D. and I do know how to deal with source materials and it is a prestigious university - and I did not feel that anything in the Dayton Accords had anything to do directly with the question that I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I don't think there are value judgements in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it the same thing would apply with the Washington Agreement. You didn't think it was necessary to look at the agreement and to see what's in the agreement, any transitional provisions in the agreement to see -- you didn't think that was necessary at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did look at the Washington Agreement, but I -- but you're right, it doesn't strike me as necessary to answer the question I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I've noticed that you've looked at some reports from the international crisis group, and they have an office in Sarajevo. They've been monitoring the situation there. They've written many, many reports, have they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They've written a lot of reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you read all of those reports or you just skimmed through it to find --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I read all of the reports dealing with Herceg-Bosna and with Bosnia in general when I was preparing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with Mostar and what have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it in those reports you would also find where they were talking about the dysfunctionality of the international community in Bosnia-Herzegovina as it's trying to implement this peace accords because of inner fighting, differences of opinion on what laws to adopt, agendas and what have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a very common theme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. With respect to Mostar - that's the last question I have - with respect to Mostar, did you ever come across any documents anywhere that called for Mostar to be the capital of -- for, for instance, the Croats, assuming that an agreement could be reached between the three constituent peoples? In any of the peace -- or any of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall reading anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. What about Okruzis? Did you ever come across that term, "Okruzi"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okruzi?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An Okruzi is probably a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And do you know how they were formed back then and who formed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back then being 1993, 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine they were formed on the local level from the ground up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have to leave it at this. I think we can end maybe one minute early today, and I do have some time from my colleagues. I might have a little time left. In total --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you've used up 45 minutes. Each of the Defence teams has 30 minutes, so I assume some of your colleagues have given you some of their time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have the full time from the Coric Defence and the full time from the Pusic Defence. So regrettably you'll have to bear with me for 45 minutes tomorrow, and I'll try and to be a little more organised than today but we've covered the difficult area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Miller, as you are under oath, you may no longer have any contact with the Prosecution. As you know, tomorrow the hearing will take place at 9.00 a.m., so I would ask you to come back. I would ask everyone here to come back and we will begin at 9.00 on the dot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
